title: About & Resources
content:
botmux connects Lark topic groups to AI coding CLIs (Claude Code, Codex and more): start a topic in a group and you get a dedicated AI session working for you. It's open source under the MIT license.

Useful links

I want to…	Go to
Read the source, file an Issue / PR	GitHub: deepcoldy/botmux
Read the docs online	deepcoldy.github.io/botmux
Install from npm	npmjs.com/package/botmux
Self-host the central platform (multiple machines, teams)	GitHub: botmux-ai/botmux-platform · Overview
Contribute	CONTRIBUTING.md
License	MIT

Install & upgrade

Recommended: one-line install script (self-contained binary, no Node needed):

curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/deepcoldy/botmux/master/install.sh | sh

Works on Linux and macOS, x64 or arm64; musl systems such as Alpine get the matching build automatically. On Windows, install inside WSL2.

Alternative: npm:

npm install -g botmux

This step needs Node ≥ 22 (an npm requirement). The npm package contains the same self-contained program, so running it doesn't need Node.

Upgrade: run botmux update (botmux upgrade is the same), then botmux restart to apply it. On releases older than v3.18.0, rerun the curl command above instead; see FAQ · How do I upgrade? for why.

New here? Start with the 5-minute quickstart; stuck? Check the FAQ.

Join the community group

Scan the QR code matching how you're joining (all join links are permanent):

Feedback

Found a problem or want a feature?

File an Issue or PR on GitHub;

or just talk to us in the Lark community group above.

This documentation was generated by botmux itself (inside a Lark topic) and is published on GitHub Pages and Lark Miaoda 🪄

title: Multi-CLI Adapters
content:
botmux is not tied to one AI coding tool. Each bot picks the CLI / agent it runs with cliId, and the adapter delivers Lark messages to it and brings the replies back. Switching CLIs means changing one field.

Local CLIs: every session is a real process on this machine. Under the default tmux backend you can tmux attach and watch it directly (pty / zellij / herdr backends differ).

API / remote agents: a few adapters (e.g. Mira App, riff, Remote Runner) don't start a local CLI process; they call a remote service. For minimal configs see API / remote adapters.

Use this page when: you want to switch the underlying CLI, wire up a new tool, or check whether a CLI accepts a model.
No new adapter needed: for gateways / launchers (aiden, ttadk, ccr, …) see Wrapper / gateway integration; for strictly Codex-compatible distributions see Codex-compatible distributions.

Switching a bot's CLI

First install the target CLI as the same system user that runs the botmux daemon, run it once in a terminal and finish its own sign-in. botmux will not sign in for you. Then pick one way:

Way	How	Takes effect
botmux setup	Pick from the CLI menu when creating or editing a bot (related CLIs are grouped into sub-menus, e.g. Codex / Codex App, TRAE 2.0 / legacy Coco)	after botmux restart
Dashboard	"Bot Config → Common → Agent Config": choose CLI and model, then "Save Agent Config"	new sessions
bots.json	Edit cliId in the entry, see bots.json	new sessions after botmux restart

Running sessions never switch CLI mid-way: cliId, wrapperCli and cliRuntime are fixed when the session is created, so a change only affects new sessions.

The Dashboard checks whether the selected CLI can be found. It looks the command up through your login shell (Zsh / Bash rc files), so a CLI that is only on the PATH set in .zshrc is still detected. When it really is missing you get a warning:

On macOS, when Codex / Codex App can't find codex on PATH, botmux also looks for the codex bundled with ChatGPT.app or Codex.app, in this order:

/Applications/ChatGPT.app/Contents/Resources/codex, ~/Applications/ChatGPT.app/Contents/Resources/codex

/Applications/Codex.app/Contents/Resources/codex, ~/Applications/Codex.app/Contents/Resources/codex

So having only the desktop app installed is enough. A codex on PATH always wins; to pin a specific one, set cliPathOverride to its absolute path. Linux has no such fallback.

Supported CLIs / agents

The table lists the built-in adapters. "Default command" is the executable botmux looks for on PATH; override it with an absolute path in cliPathOverride. The authoritative list is src/adapters/cli/registry.ts.

cliId	CLI / agent	Default command	Integration	model
claude-code	Claude Code (default)	claude	local process	✅
codex	Codex CLI	codex	local process	✅
codex-app	Codex App	codex	local process (app-server protocol)	✅
cursor	Cursor (cursor-agent)	cursor-agent	local process	✅
opencode	OpenCode	opencode	local process	✅
opencode2	OpenCode 2 (beta)	opencode2	local process	
mimocode	MiMoCode	mimo	local process	✅
antigravity	Antigravity	agy	local process	✅
copilot	GitHub Copilot	copilot	local process	✅
grok	Grok Build	grok	local process	✅
kimi	Kimi Code	kimi	local process	✅
kiro-cli	Kiro	kiro-cli	local process	
reasonix	Reasonix	reasonix	local process	✅
zcode	ZCode	zcode	local process	✅
doubao	Doubao CLI (see Doubao guide)	doubao	local process	✅
pi	Pi	pi	local process	✅
oh-my-pi	Oh My Pi (Pi fork)	omp	local process	✅
aiden	Aiden (native agent)	aiden	local process	
traex	TRAE CLI 2.0 (traex)	traex	local process	✅
coco	TRAE CLI 1.0 / CoCo (legacy, no longer maintained; requires ≥ 0.120.32)	coco	local process	✅
mtr	MTR	mtr	local process	
hermes	Hermes	hermes	local process	
ebsd	EBSD (requires credential files, see guide)	ebsd	local process	
codem	CodeM (see CodeM guide)	codem	local process	✅
minimax	MiniMax Code / mcode (see MiniMax guide)	mcode	local process	✅
genius	Genius	genius	local process	✅
seed	Seed (Claude Code fork)	seed	local process	✅
relay	Relay (new release of Seed)	relay	local process	✅
dsh	DeepSeek Harness (see below)	dsh	local process (SDK JSON-RPC)	✅
mir	Mir CLI (local mircli, see below)	mircli	local process	
mira	Mira App	none	API / remote	
riff	riff	none	cloud agent (API)	
mojo	Mojo	mojo	API-driven (host execution / cloud sandbox)	✅
remote-runner	Generic Remote Runner (see protocol)	botmux-remote-runner	remote protocol	✅

About the model column

✅ means the model really is passed to the CLI at launch. You can set a default model for the bot in bots.json / the Dashboard, or pick one for a single new topic with /t … /model <model> in its first message (see Slash commands).

For CLIs without ✅, the model is decided by the CLI's own config or UI. The model field is ignored, and /model in a topic header is rejected outright rather than silently dropped.

riff is the exception: its model only comes from the bot's riff config block, not from model.

Some CLIs accept a model but ship no built-in candidate list (e.g. Seed, Relay, Pi). Setup won't prompt for a model; type one in if needed, or switch with the CLI's native /model.

Gemini CLI has been removed

Gemini CLI is no longer maintained upstream, so botmux removed the gemini adapter, and the Dashboard and botmux setup no longer offer it. The replacement is antigravity (Antigravity, command agy).

A bot whose bots.json entry still says cliId: "gemini" refuses to start, with a hint to change it to "antigravity". Other bots keep running.

In scripted setup, the old Gemini number 6 now reports an error instead of selecting another CLI.

To migrate:
Install agy and sign in with a Google account; or skip the sign-in and use a Gemini API key: set "modelProvider": "gemini" in ~/.gemini/antigravity-cli/settings.json and provide GEMINI_API_KEY.

Change cliId to "antigravity" (edit bots.json, or change the bot's CLI with botmux setup).

Remove or reconfigure Gemini-only settings: cliPathOverride / wrapperCli (e.g. ttadk gemini), Gemini model names, GEMINI_CLI_HOME.

Run botmux restart.

While the bot is not started, the Dashboard can only show the reason; it cannot save that bot's settings.

Wrapper / gateway integration

Often you don't run the native CLI directly but through a gateway or launcher (intranet proxy + SSO, model routing, …). No new adapter is needed: keep cliId set to the real underlying CLI (claude-code, codex, …) and only change how it is launched. Reply capture, session resume, hooks and the rest keep working.

Option 1: a wrapperCli launch prefix (recommended)

Set wrapperCli on the bot, and botmux launches <wrapperCli> <CLI args>. No script needed, works on every OS.

{
  "cliId": "claude-code",
  "wrapperCli": "aiden x claude"
}

The botmux setup and Dashboard CLI menus already include common combinations and fill this in for you:

Menu item	cliId	wrapperCli
Aiden × Claude / Aiden × Codex	claude-code / codex	aiden x claude / aiden x codex
CJADK × Claude / CJADK × Codex	claude-code / codex	cjadk claude / cjadk codex
TTADK × Claude / Codex / OpenCode / CoCo / Cursor	matching CLI	ttadk claude, etc.

Notes:

The first word is looked up on PATH and replaces the CLI's default command; with wrapperCli set, cliPathOverride no longer applies.

aiden x claude rejects the --settings botmux injects, so botmux strips it automatically; other launchers get the args unchanged.

For TTADK combinations, the bot's model field is passed as ttadk -m <model> (defaults to glm-5.1 when empty; TTADK × CoCo takes no model).

Any other launcher such as ccr works too.

wrapperCli cannot be combined with cliRuntime.

Option 2: your own wrapper script + cliPathOverride

When launching is more involved (changing env vars, stripping args, forcing a PTY, …), write a script:

Sign in to the gateway first (once), as the same system user that runs the daemon. An expired token pops an interactive login that blocks the terminal, so keep the session alive.

Write the script in ~/.botmux/bin/ and forward botmux's arguments to the real CLI. Some gateways reject --settings; strip it in the script.

chmod +x (the most commonly missed step). Without the executable bit you get EACCES, the CLI exits right away and the bot keeps restarting.

Run the script directly to verify: ~/.botmux/bin/xxx --version. Don't test with bash xxx; that doesn't need the executable bit and hides the problem in step 3.

Set cliPathOverride in bots.json to the script's absolute path (not ~), then botmux restart.

Follow each gateway team's published docs for the actual script. MTR is community-contributed; install with npm i -g @metamove-code/mtr-cli@latest.

Debugging a wrapper: find the Spawning fresh CLI: line in botmux logs, copy the full command and run it by hand in a terminal. That usually shows whether it's permissions, arguments or sign-in.

Codex-compatible distributions

If you run a separately released distribution that is strictly compatible with Codex, use cliId: "codex" plus cliRuntime: cliId selects the Codex protocol adapter and cliRuntime names the binary that actually runs. It reuses model args, session resume, idle detection and Codex RPC, without being version-checked as official Codex.

"Strictly compatible" means it accepts the arguments botmux passes to Codex, keeps the same interactive states and rollout / resume semantics, and uses a compatible auth / home layout. If it changes arguments, the UI state machine, session storage or the protocol, contribute a real adapter instead.

In the Dashboard, switch "Codex Runtime" to "Custom Compatible" and fill in the executable and update source:

For all fields and update sources see the Codex-compatible distributions section of bots.json. The older cliPathOverride setup keeps working, but it does not turn on Codex RPC features that require an explicit compatibility declaration.

API / remote adapters {#remote-agents}

The agents behind these four adapters don't run in a local terminal. riff, mojo and remote-runner are paired with the session backend of the same name automatically, so you don't need to set backendType.

cliId	Minimal config	Sign-in
mira	cliId only	reads the local Mira.app login cookie
riff	cliId + riff.baseUrl	a JWT, or the local ByteCloud sign-in
mojo	cliId only, with mojo on PATH	local mojo auth login, or an injected JWT
remote-runner	cliId, plus cliPathOverride when the provider isn't called botmux-remote-runner	handled by the provider

Mira App

In botmux setup, choose Mira → Mira App (Web API); this writes cliId: "mira". botmux calls Mira's Web API through a built-in runner, so no CLI is needed.

{ "cliId": "mira" }

Sign-in:

By default, open Mira.app on macOS and sign in. botmux uses the sqlite3 command to read mira_session from ~/Library/Application Support/mira/Cookies, so sqlite3 must be installed.

Not on macOS, or the cookies live elsewhere: set MIRA_COOKIE_HEADER (a full Cookie header) or MIRA_SESSION (just the mira_session value) in the daemon environment or the bot's env, or point MIRA_COOKIE_DB at the cookie database. These are credentials; never post them in chat.

Without a cookie you get "Open Mira.app and sign in". The model ignores the model field and follows Mira's own settings. The local Mir CLI is a separate adapter; see Mir CLI and the MCP Bridge.

riff

riff runs the agent in a cloud sandbox, so nothing is installed locally. riff.baseUrl is required; use the riff service address for your environment:

{
  "cliId": "riff",
  "riff": { "baseUrl": "https://riff.example.internal" }
}

You can also pick Riff as the CLI under "Agent Config" in the Dashboard and fill in the "Riff backend config" panel that appears. Common optional fields:

Field	Description
model	Model used in the sandbox; empty means riff's default. The bot's top-level model has no effect on riff
reasoningEffort	low / medium / high / xhigh; empty means the default
sandboxCluster	Sandbox pool for new tasks: boe or cn

Sign-in (the JWT is looked up in this order on every riff call):

riff.jwt holds the token directly. Not recommended: it's stored in plain text and expires quickly.

The environment variable named by riff.jwtEnv, RIFF_JWT by default. Set it in the daemon's environment and renew it yourself.

Neither set (recommended): on the daemon machine, sign in once to a ByteCloud CLI as the same system user, and botmux reads the sign-in it stores locally, skipping expired tokens.

On a 401, sign in again on the daemon machine; no restart needed. riff can only be configured per bot; you can't switch a topic to it with /t.

Mojo

With mojo on PATH and signed in on this machine, cliId alone is enough:

{ "cliId": "mojo" }

Sign in one of two ways:

Run mojo auth login as the same system user that runs the daemon.

Inject a JWT: put the token in mojo.jwt, or name the environment variable to read with mojo.jwtEnv (default X_JWT_TOKEN). An injected JWT takes priority over the local sign-in.

Tools run on this host by default; set mojo.cloud: true to run them in the cloud sandbox instead. Put the model in the bot's top-level model. Fields such as bin, cwd, model and wrapperCli are rejected inside the mojo block; use the top-level cliPathOverride, workingDir, model and wrapperCli.

Remote Runner

Remote Runner connects any remote agent platform over a JSONL protocol. botmux starts a provider subprocess, and the provider owns the remote resources and the sign-in:

{
  "cliId": "remote-runner",
  "cliPathOverride": "/opt/example/bin/my-remote-runner"
}

Without cliPathOverride, botmux looks for botmux-remote-runner on PATH.

The provider reads its own credentials, injected via a permission-restricted file or the deployment environment, e.g. a token file path in the bot's env. The remoteRunner block holds no credentials, and unknown fields in it are rejected.

The remoteRunner block is optional and describes protocol expectations:

Field	Description
expectedProvider	Provider name checked during the handshake
requiredCapabilities	Capabilities the provider must declare; it won't start without them
handshakeTimeoutMs	Limit for the handshake and for start / resume to reach ready; integer, 100–300000 ms
operationTimeoutMs	Limit for status / cancel / detach; integer, 100–300000 ms

envPolicy.mode: "strict" is not supported for Remote Runner and fails at startup. For protocol details see the Remote Runner protocol.

Notes for specific CLIs

Using the newly added CLIs {#new-clis}

Grok Build, Reasonix, OpenCode 2, DeepSeek Harness (dsh / dsh-tui), MiniMax Code (mcode), MiMoCode, CodeM, ZCode and Doubao are all built-in adapters with no extra switch. Turning one on works like switching to any other CLI (see Switching a bot's CLI above): install the command and log in under the daemon's system user, then set the bot's cliId to the value below.

CLI	cliId	Default command
Grok Build	grok	grok
Reasonix	reasonix	reasonix
OpenCode 2 (beta)	opencode2	opencode2
DeepSeek Harness	dsh	dsh (for the full-screen TUI also set dshRuntime: "tui", which launches dsh-tui; see below)
MiniMax Code	minimax	mcode
MiMoCode	mimocode	mimo
CodeM	codem	codem
ZCode	zcode	zcode
Doubao	doubao	doubao

Forge × TraeX: to start TraeX through Forge, pick Forge x TraeX in the CLI menu of botmux setup or the Dashboard, or write "cliId": "traex", "cliLaunchMode": "forge-traex" in bots.json. botmux then launches forge run --agent traex --agent-args ..., so forge must be on PATH. This launch mode only works with cliId: "traex" and can't be combined with wrapperCli, cliRuntime, cliPathOverride, the file sandbox or readIsolation; such configs are rejected.

TraeX automatic model switching (experimental) {#traex-auto-model}

A TraeX bot can set model to auto and provide an ordered model pool. A session starts on the first model and moves on to later models in the pool when it queues or runs out of quota. Switching restarts TraeX and resumes the same session; inputs already sent are not replayed.

In the Dashboard, choose TraeX under "Agent Config", tick "Experimental: automatic model switching" and order the models; each model can have its own reasoning effort and context:

The matching bots.json:

{
  "cliId": "traex",
  "model": "auto",
  "traexAutoModel": {
    "enabled": true,
    "models": ["model-a", "model-b"],
    "queueTimeoutMs": 30000
  }
}

Field	Description
enabled	Must be true
models	The pool, in order. The first is preferred, the rest are fallbacks. Only these models are used; no duplicates, and auto is not allowed
trigger	When to switch: capacity (model queueing, default) or quota (explicit quota exhaustion)
queueTimeoutMs	How long sustained queueing lasts before switching; 5000–300000 ms, default 30000
switchCooldownMs	Minimum time since the last switch before a new queue episode can switch again; 5000–300000 ms, default 60000
reselectPerTurn	Default false: later inputs in a topic keep the selected model. With true, every new input starts again from the preferred model
preflightLoadCheck	Default false. With true, load is checked before each independent new turn and an overloaded model is switched out. capacity mode only
overloadThresholdPercent	Overload threshold for the preflight check, default 100; only load above it counts as overloaded
preflightTimeoutMs	Timeout for the preflight check; 100–30000 ms, default 8000
modelSettings	Per-model settings, e.g. {"model-a": {"reasoningEffort": "xhigh", "modelBackendVariant": "max"}}

The two triggers:

Capacity queue (capacity): after queueing for queueTimeoutMs, switch to the first later model with load at or below 100% (or unknown load). When all later models are above 100%, pick the lowest-load model in the pool (ties go by pool order) and wait there without further switching; when loads are incomplete, try each model in order and finally pick the one with the best queue position.

Quota exhausted (quota): only structured quota-exhaustion errors count; ordinary 429s, queueing, network or auth failures never trigger it. Models known to be out of quota are skipped; when all are exhausted, automatic retries stop and the next independent input checks again.

Things to know:

Only applies to cliId: "traex". If model is auto but traexAutoModel is missing or invalid, botmux logs a warning and passes no model to TraeX, so TraeX's own default is used.

New topics start on the preferred model. In quota mode, every new independent input starts on the first model that still has quota, regardless of reselectPerTurn.

Changes apply to newly started or restarted sessions.

Pi execution progress

Bots with cliId: "pi" show Pi's persisted thinking, narration, tool calls and results in the Lark progress bubble. Tool nodes show commands or file paths and finish with the current turn; the final answer is still sent as a reply.

On by default; respects cotEnabled and the chat's /cot on / /cot off. /cot show displays what the current turn has accumulated.

Updates follow complete messages written by Pi: tool calls appear before they run, results after they finish, not token by token.

History is not replayed into a new turn's bubble.

DeepSeek Harness (dsh)

cliId: "dsh" drives the local dsh CLI (deepseek-harness) through a built-in runner, using the SDK JSON-RPC protocol of dsh --profile <name>. Reasoning and tool activity show up in the card's thinking section.

Prerequisites:

dsh is on PATH (or set via cliPathOverride). It must be the dsh command from the npm package @deepseek-ai/dsh; early versions used dsh-jsonrpc-agent from a Python package, and having only that old command on PATH gives "command not found".

Configure and sign in with native dsh first. The data dir is $DSH_HOME, or ~/.dsh when unset.

The profile is botmux by default (override per bot with dshProfile) and lives in $DSH_HOME/profiles/<name>/.

No need to create the profile by hand: if it's missing, botmux writes a minimal skeleton (package.json, empty cordis.yml, cordis.patch.yml) and runs dsh plugin add to install dependencies. The default patch disables the web plugins that would block startup in headless mode and inserts the SDK JSON-RPC server; the default botmux profile also gets the ask_user_question tool. Everything else comes from dsh-base.

To add community plugins or switch model providers, edit that profile's cordis.patch.yml; botmux only creates the file when it's missing and never overwrites it. When editing:

- insert: [...] adds plugins;

a bare - id: X (no insert) overrides the config of an existing plugin and is silently skipped if the id doesn't exist.

How the model is chosen: botmux takes agent-default-model from the composed profile; explicit values in the legacy $DSH_HOME/settings.yaml win while that file exists; with neither, it uses deepseek-official / deepseek-v4-flash. A bot model only overrides the model name; the provider still comes from the config above.

Other points:

DSH_HOME can only be set in the daemon's environment; a per-bot env.DSH_HOME is rejected to avoid split profile paths.

Session logs go to $DSH_HOME/sessions/botmux/. Turns within one runner share context; after a daemon restart a new session starts without the old context.

For the full-screen TUI instead of the runner: keep cliId: "dsh" and set dshRuntime: "tui" (also switchable in the Dashboard). It then launches the dsh-tui command; the model comes from the TUI's own config and /model, and the TUI's state lives in ~/.dsh-tui.

When the model calls ask_user_question, a Lark question card pops up. In TUI mode Lark is tried first, and questions a card can't represent fall back to the native TUI. To turn the bridge off, set BOTMUX_DSH_ASK_BRIDGE=0 and restart the session.

Mir CLI and the MCP Bridge

In botmux setup, choosing Mira → Mir CLI (local mircli) writes cliId: "mir" (the other item, "Mira App (Web API)", is cliId: "mira"). It runs mircli -p --lean locally, so the system user that runs the daemon must have finished Mir CLI sign-in and initialization. The rules are the same on DevBox, macOS and other Linux machines:

botmux can find mircli, or cliPathOverride points to its absolute path.

~/.mira/config.json already has a device_id (usually written by mircli mcp --device-id <id> or Mir CLI's own setup).

miramcp is in Mir CLI's standard location (e.g. ~/.local/bin/miramcp), or MIRAMCP_BIN points to it.

Before calling mircli for a message, botmux tries to start the MCP Bridge:

miramcp run --device-id <device_id>

If it's already running (checked via ~/.mira/miramcp/miramcp.pid and local port 9801), it isn't started again. To check its status:

mircli mcp status

To stop the auto-start, either put this in ~/.mira/config.json:

{"auto_start_bridge": false}

or disable it for the botmux process only:

MIRCLI_AUTO_START_MIRAMCP=0 botmux start

Doubao CLI

cliId: "doubao" bridges the interactive UI of the local Doubao CLI. Install it and sign in as the same system user first:

npm install -g '@bytedance/doubao-cli' --registry=https://registry.npmjs.org
doubao          # sign in, wait for the input box, then /exit
botmux setup    # choose Doubao as the CLI, then the project directory

model is optional; when set, use the name shown in the native /model menu. Press Esc in the web terminal to interrupt the current turn. botmux launches it with --permission-mode always_allow by default, so keep it to trusted users and projects. See the Doubao guide for intranet installs and limitations.

Codex App native questions

In codex-app sessions (and codex sessions with app-server RPC enabled), when the model calls native request_user_input, botmux turns the question into a Lark question card. Pick on the card, or reply with text in the session, and the answer goes back to the same native turn; no new prompt needed. TRAE RPC uses the same bridge.

(Rendered locally from real card JSON; for illustration only.)

Answering:

All questions in one request share a card, with option descriptions shown per question; a recommended option is never auto-selected, you have to submit it.

If the batch contains a free-text question, the whole batch is answered with one text reply in the session.

Choice questions need at least two options; secret-input questions and malformed questions fail outright, with no partial answers. Never type passwords or other secrets in chat.

Who may answer follows the existing Ask routing and reply permissions.

Waiting and cancellation:

Waits up to one hour. A failed card, timeout, expired card or unrepresentable question interrupts the original turn, so the agent never continues on an empty answer.

Waiting is cancelled when the turn ends, the process exits or the session closes; late answers are not delivered.

After a daemon restart these requests are not retried or restored.

Async questions (request_user_input_async, codex-app only):

The model can keep working after asking; the card can still be answered after the original turn ends normally. Answers keep the original call ID and question indexes.

With codexAppCleanInput on, the original turn still running and steered input supported, the asker's answer joins the original turn directly; otherwise a new turn starts in the same thread. Late answers never join a different task.

A card showing "Ended" means the answers were collected, not that the model has read them.

Reply permissions: for human-started turns, the single answerer is locked when the card is registered; scheduled / autonomous turns let members with talk permission (canTalk) answer, while the schedule creator still needs operate permission (canOperate), and silent schedules don't show a card; for doc-comment turns only the original commenter can answer, in a private chat.

With several pending cards, a text answer must quote the target card; unquoted messages are treated as normal input and you get a hint to disambiguate.

Pending cards are not restored across daemon / runner restarts, and past questions are not resent.

Not covered by this bridge: Workflow sub-tasks (use humanGate / decision nodes), API-only sessions without a Lark channel, plain terminal-paste mode, and the App history viewer. Whether the native tool is available ultimately depends on the Codex version and mode.

To test: in a normal Codex App session, ask the model to use request_user_input for a choice question, check that the card arrives in Lark, then submit and confirm the same turn continues and can repeat your choice.

Steering a running Codex App turn {#codex-app-steer}

Only for cliId: "codex-app" sessions; on by default with nothing to configure on the Lark side. While Codex App is running a turn, a new message you send in the topic is injected into the current turn (Codex turn/steer) instead of waiting in the queue. When it lands, the bot replies "Got it — guidance accepted". Handy for "also handle X" or "stop that, do Y instead" mid-task.

Only messages sent directly by people steer. Messages from other bots queue as usual unless @steer is the first semantic line of the body (it may follow the line that @mentions the recipient).

If it can't be injected (for example, the turn is wrapping up), the message is queued like a normal one; nothing is lost.

Tasks triggered through the HTTP API must pass steer: true in options explicitly, starting with the first turn; see API task trigger.

Claude Code busy/idle detection (OSC 7501) {#claude-osc-7501}

Automatic, nothing to configure. The Claude Code adapter supports the OSC 7501 program status protocol: as soon as the CLI reports its first valid status, "working / idle" follows that report instead of guessing from the terminal screen, so card status and "turn ended" are more accurate. Until a status arrives, the screen is still used. The Pi and Kimi adapters use the same protocol.

Adding a new adapter (contributors)

Create a file under src/adapters/cli/ implementing the CliAdapter interface.

Add the new ID to the CliId union in src/adapters/cli/types.ts.

Add the import, switch case and export in src/adapters/cli/registry.ts.

Add a display name to CLI_DISPLAY_NAMES in src/adapters/cli/display-names.ts (shared by cards, setup and the Dashboard; missing it fails compilation).

Add a number to CLI_ID_CHOICES in src/setup/bot-config-editor.ts, always appended at the end: the numbers are a stable interface for scripted setup, and inserting in the middle makes old scripts silently pick the wrong CLI. The setup menu and Dashboard dropdown follow automatically.

Update the CLI list in README.md and README.en.md.

File-sandbox support also needs the CLI's state directories declared correctly; see src/adapters/cli/CLAUDE.md and CONTRIBUTING.md.

toc.text: Mir CLI and the MCP Bridge
Steering a running Codex App turn

description: botmux is not tied to one AI coding tool. Each bot picks the CLI / agent it runs with cliId, and the adapter delivers Lark messages to it and brings the replies back. Switching CLIs means changing one field. Local CLIs: every session is a real process on this machine. Under the default tmux backend you can tmux attach and watch it directly (pty / zellij / herdr backends differ).API / remote agents: a few adapters (e.g. Mira App, riff, Remote Runner) don't start a local CLI process; they call a remote service. For minimal configs see API / remote adapters. Use this page when: you want to switch the underlying CLI, wire up a new tool, or check whether a CLI accepts a model. No new adapter needed: for gateways / launchers (aiden, ttadk, ccr, …) see Wrapper / gateway integration; for strictly Codex-compatible distributions see Codex-compatible distributions.

title: Session Adopt
content:
Your CLI is halfway through a task and you have to leave? Send /adopt in Lark to bring that already-running CLI into the current topic: watch progress and keep sending messages from your phone, and find everything unchanged when you're back at your desk.

Supported terminals: tmux, Zellij, Herdr, and Orca (experimental). The same card also lists past sessions of the bot's CLI, so you can resume one into the current topic.

<video src={video_v3_adopt_relay_en} controls preload="metadata" style={{width:'100%',borderRadius:'8px'}}>

Quick start

Start your CLI (for example, Claude Code) as usual in tmux / Zellij / Herdr on your machine.

In Lark, send /adopt to a bot bound to the same CLI.

A "📡 Choose a CLI session to adopt" card appears: tap a session to select it, then tap the confirm button below.

After "📡 Adopted …", messages you send in the topic are typed straight into that terminal, and the terminal's output and answers sync back to Lark.

To skip the card, name the target directly:

/adopt                 # Scan and show the selection card
/adopt 0:2.0           # Adopt a tmux pane (session:window.pane)
/adopt mysess:3        # Adopt a Zellij pane (session:paneId, or session/paneId)
/adopt <Herdr pane ID> # Adopt a Herdr pane
/adopt orca:term_xxx   # Adopt an Orca terminal (experimental)
/adopt <session ID>    # Resume a past session (the CLI's own session ID)

What's on the selection card

The card mixes two kinds of candidates and supports search (title / project / path) and paging:

Source	What it is	Confirm button	Result
🟢 Running	A local CLI currently running in tmux / Zellij / Herdr / Orca	Take over into this topic	Bridged to the original terminal; the process keeps running
🕘 History	A session of the same CLI saved on disk that can be resumed	Resume into this topic	Botmux relaunches the CLI with --resume; it becomes a normal Botmux session

Each candidate shows the CLI, path, uptime (or last activity), and "Location". For tmux, Zellij, and Herdr the heading is the workspace or tab name and "Location" holds the session / pane locator; Orca headings use the terminal or CLI session title.

Filtering rules:

Only the bot's own CLI is listed: a Pi bot won't list Codex or TRAE panes, so the CLI behind the bot never changes silently.

Botmux's own sessions are hidden: persistent bmx-* sessions and any session Botmux already manages (open or closed) are excluded. To bring back a Botmux session you closed, use "Resume session" on its session card.

A running session never shows up again under History.

History lists at most the 20 most recent sessions. Use search to narrow it down, or run /adopt <session ID> directly.

Only the person who summoned the card can use it. Others should send their own /adopt.

CLIs that support History: Claude Code, Codex, TRAE CLI, Grok, OpenCode / OpenCode 2, Antigravity, Genius. For other CLIs the card shows live sessions only.

After adopting: a bridge, not a takeover

When you adopt a live session, Botmux only observes and writes input to the target terminal. It never changes the original terminal's focus, layout, or size.

Both sides stay in sync: messages from Lark are typed into the terminal, and terminal output appears on the streaming card in real time. On adoption you first get a "📜 Last exchange before /adopt" card so you know where things stand; anything you type directly in the terminal also syncs to Lark as a "🖥️ Local terminal turn".

Disconnect any time: tap "⏏ Disconnect" on the streaming card, or send /detach (alias /disconnect; /close in an adopted topic does the same). Botmux removes only its own side and never ends your CLI; the original process keeps running locally.

One adopted session per topic: sending /adopt again in a topic that already has one asks you to disconnect first.

The old "🔄 Take Over" button is retired: new cards don't show it, and tapping it on an old card does nothing. Today adopt has a single form, the shared bridge.

Resuming a past session

Pick a "🕘 History" entry on the card, or send /adopt <session ID>. Botmux relaunches the CLI with --resume in the original working directory and picks up that conversation. Unlike the bridge, Botmux now starts and manages the CLI, just like any new session (it can be restarted, and closing it ends the process).

If the ID belongs to a Botmux session:

In the current topic → it's resumed directly.

In another topic → it isn't moved here. You're asked to tap "Resume session" in the original topic, or run botmux resume <id> locally.

Notes for Codex users

Drafts are never overwritten. If the adopted Codex terminal has an unsubmitted local draft, Botmux keeps the draft, doesn't append the Lark message, and asks you to submit or clear it in the terminal before resending. Orca terminals behave the same way, and Botmux also stops if it can't reach Orca to confirm the composer is empty.

When Codex uses a shared background server, Botmux still types into the original tmux pane. We recommend enabling thread-id (legacy name session-id) in Codex's /statusline and keeping the full ID visible. Botmux uses it to confirm which session received your message and to follow /new or /resume switches you make in the terminal.

Codex App conversations. If the bot's CLI is codex-app, /adopt lists existing Codex App conversations instead ("📱 Choose a Codex App conversation"). Pick one to continue that thread in the topic, or send /adopt <threadId> (an ID prefix works too).

Sharing a Codex App on your dev machine (experimental). To have Lark and the desktop Codex App connected to the same App Server and the same thread at once, add this to a bot whose cliId is codex or codex-app:

{
  "existingAppServer": { "endpoint": "unix:///absolute/path/app-server.sock" }
}

endpoint accepts local addresses only: a unix:// socket with an absolute path, or ws://127.0.0.1:<port>. Then pick a conversation with /adopt to share it. Botmux never creates or stops the App Server; /detach disconnects only the Lark side, and the App Server and Codex App session keep running. Avoid submitting different tasks from both sides at the same time. If the remote terminal shows "Hooks need review" the first time, choose "Continue without trusting" in the Web Terminal; Botmux won't trust all hooks for you. This mode can't be combined with codexBrowser, codexRpcInput, or wrapperCli.

Orca (experimental)

Orca works in two modes:

Server mode: a persistent orcad on Linux, with its CLI at ~/.orca/cli/bin/orca.

SSH relay mode: when Botmux and the SSH terminal run on the same Linux host, Botmux connects directly to the local relay that owns the original PTY. This route doesn't need the desktop client, so you can close your Mac and still send /adopt to get back to the session. Cross-host relays still go through the desktop, which must stay online.

Things to know:

Before adopting, Botmux checks the terminal's identity (handle, PTY incarnation, workspace, local process ownership). Terminals without a stable identity are neither listed nor restored, so a reused terminal handle can't receive your input. Older relays without incarnation data can't use the direct route.

Sessions previously adopted through the desktop relay need one more /adopt to switch to the direct local route.

The Web Terminal shows a text screen: you can view and type, but source colors, exact cursor state, and mouse modes aren't kept. After the desktop disconnects, the screen is rebuilt from retained output; if that output starts in the middle of a redraw, the screen may be incomplete.

Orca/relay versions, terminal redraw behavior, and each CLI's transcript format affect compatibility. If sessions stop being listed, or the screen or replies look wrong after an upgrade, adopt again and report your version details.

What each CLI gets

CLI	What works
Claude Code, Codex, TRAE	Terminal I/O + structured replies + scrollable history rebuilt from the transcript
MTR, Hermes, and other unverified CLIs	Basic terminal access only: live screen, Lark input, and Web Terminal work; structured replies and scrollable history aren't guaranteed

The last row isn't a terminal I/O limitation. Botmux simply can't reliably prove which transcript belongs to that terminal: MTR can't tell sessions apart when several share one directory, and an externally started Hermes session has no Botmux session marker. Botmux won't guess from "the newest session in the same directory", because that could send another terminal's conversation to Lark.

Limits

An adopted process runs on your machine and its lifecycle isn't Botmux's to manage, so these boundaries apply:

Action	Result
/relay to another group	Not supported. To continue elsewhere, start a new session and hand off
Fork, restart, or resume an adopted session	Not supported; Botmux won't touch your tmux pane or CLI process
The CLI exits on its own	The session ends with it ("⏏ Adopted CLI session has exited.") and isn't relaunched
/adopt on a bot with the file sandbox on	Rejected. A sandbox can only be applied at launch, not wrapped around a running process; sending a message instead starts a new sandboxed session
The topic is waiting for you to pick a repo	Tap "Close session" on the card first, then /adopt again
/dismiss while the group has an adopted session	The group isn't disbanded. /detach in that topic first, then /dismiss

After a daemon restart, Botmux first checks whether the adopted CLI is still there:

Confirmed gone → the session is closed.

Still running → it's reattached automatically, without posting a recovery card.

Can't tell right now (for example, a transient probe failure) → the session isn't closed, but it's held without reattaching. It's checked again on the next daemon restart, not automatically when your next message arrives.

Typical usage

Claude Code is running in tmux on your office computer and you have to leave: send /adopt from Lark on your phone → pick the session → confirm, and it syncs right away. Keep watching and sending on the road; back at your desk, tap "⏏ Disconnect" and carry on in the terminal. It's not remote control; it's one session shared across devices.

Related pages: Slash commands, Relay, File sandbox, tmux.

title: Core-only (apiOnly) API Control
content:
Want to embed botmux in your own system and drive a CLI over HTTP, without touching Feishu? Use core-only.
It is botmux as one process, on a fixed port, listening only on 127.0.0.1: no Feishu credentials, no bots.json, no supervisor or dashboard. Your orchestrator (task runner, CI, backend service, sandbox) asks it over HTTP to run a CLI (codex / claude-code / …), polls the result, and opens a web terminal when it needs to see what's happening.

This page is for integrators embedding botmux into their own product, for example a botmux inside a sandbox running codex.

If you only want an external system to trigger a normal bot already running in a Feishu group, see Triggering Tasks via API. The two pages complement each other: the request body, idempotency and polling states work exactly the same under core-only. This page only covers what's specific to core-only: startup, readiness, interrupting a turn, the web terminal, auth, and the security boundary.

Two related entry points: to start sessions and fetch results from a local script or CI, use Headless Automation Sessions; to let OpenAI-protocol tools reuse a CLI's model login, use Model Proxy (it runs a core-only instance underneath).

At a glance

Your orchestrator                         botmux serve --api-only (127.0.0.1:8930)
─────────────────                         ─────────────────────────────────────────
1. Start the process, wait for       ──▶  bind port → restore old sessions → print ready line
   GET /healthz → 200
2. POST /api/trigger (async)         ──▶  start the CLI (codex / claude-code …) on the task
                                     ◀──  { sessionId, triggerId }
3. GET  …/trigger-result (poll)      ──▶  running → completed / failed / interrupted
   (optional) POST …/turns/<triggerId>/interrupt  stop only this turn, keep the session
4. (optional) GET …/write-link       ──▶  returns an interactive web terminal URL
   (signed)

A typical integration only needs steps 1–3, and none of them require signing.

1. How it differs from normal botmux

botmux start (fleet)	botmux serve --api-only (core-only)
Processes	supervisor + dashboard + one daemon per bot	one process, in the foreground; the service lives as long as the process
Feishu credentials	larkAppSecret required	not needed at all; never connects to Feishu
Bot config	~/.botmux/bots.json / BOTS_CONFIG	ignores both; generates exactly one apiOnly bot (still reads the global ~/.botmux/.env and global config)
Where results go	replies posted to a Feishu topic	nothing is sent to Feishu; results are only available over HTTP
Port	probes upward if taken	fixed port, 127.0.0.1 only, exits if it can't bind
Data directory	~/.botmux/data	its own ~/.botmux/core-only/<botId>/data

In one line: core-only is a headless, single-tenant, loopback-only botmux. It keeps the full daemon HTTP interface and just drops the Feishu side.

2. Startup

# Recommended: the CLI subcommand. Runs in the foreground and inherits stdout,
# so your launcher can watch for the ready line
BOTMUX_API_PORT=8930 botmux serve --api-only

# Same thing with flags
botmux serve --api-only --port 8930 --cli codex --working-dir /path/to/repo

# With an npm install you can also run the entry file directly (for embedded spawn;
# the single-file binary has no dist/, so use the subcommand above)
BOTMUX_API_PORT=8930 node <pkg>/dist/index-core-only.js

Flags and env vars (a flag wins when both are given):

Flag	Env var	Default	Meaning
--port	BOTMUX_API_PORT	none, required	Listen port; exits if it can't bind
--bot	BOTMUX_API_ONLY_BOT	local_riff	Bot id; must look like local_<name> (letters, digits, ., _, -)
--cli	BOTMUX_CORE_CLI	codex-app	Which CLI to run, e.g. codex, claude-code
--working-dir	BOTMUX_CORE_WORKING_DIR	current directory	The CLI's working directory
--state-dir	BOTMUX_CORE_STATE_DIR	~/.botmux/core-only/<botId>/data	Where session data lives
--backend	BOTMUX_CORE_BACKEND	tmux	tmux or pty. Pick pty only if the host can't run a reliable tmux server; with pty the terminal can't be reattached after a daemon restart
none	BOTMUX_CORE_MODEL	unset	Override the default model
none	BOTMUX_CORE_CODEX_AUTH_SYNC	unset (shared)	Set to isolated to make Codex use only this bot's own CODEX_HOME, never reading or copying the machine's global login

Which CLI?

codex-app (default): runs through the app-server, returns structured results, no visible terminal.

codex, claude-code, etc.: run the real TUI in tmux, which you can watch or take over through the web terminal (see section 4).

When is it "up"?

The daemon binds the port first, then restores old sessions. A port that accepts connections isn't ready for tasks yet — wait for readiness:

The stdout ready line (fixed format; match with the regex ^\[core-only\] listening on ), printed only after restore completes:

[core-only] listening on 127.0.0.1:8930 (bot local_riff, cli codex-app)

GET /healthz (no signing):
not ready → 503 {"ok":false,"status":"starting"}

ready → 200 {"ok":true}

While not ready, /api/trigger, trigger-result, insight, host-facts and the interrupt route also return 503 starting right away, so even if you skip the probe you can't send a task into a session that is still being restored. Still, the recommended flow is: poll /healthz until 200, then send the first task.

/__health is public too, but it always returns 200. It only tells you the process is alive, not whether it can take tasks.

3. Running tasks: trigger, poll, interrupt

For the full request body, idempotency keys and polling states, see Triggering Tasks via API. Core-only adds a few rules:

Rule	Details
An HTTP response mode is required	Set options.waitForFinalOutput (wait for the result) or options.asyncReturnSessionId (get a sessionId back). With neither → 400 bad_request, since there's no Feishu group to reply into
No Feishu targets	A real Feishu chatId or rootMessageId → 400
You can continue your own session	target.sessionId must be one of this service's own sessions; use it to add another turn to the same session
The instruction goes in top-level instruction	Not prompt
Poll with the full sessionId	It's a UUID, not the [worker:xxxxxxxx] short tag in the logs; the short tag gives session_not_found
options.model / options.reasoningEffort	Only apply to CLIs that support switching model / reasoning effort, and only for new sessions; see the trigger docs

Trigger and poll

# Trigger (async): no signing
curl -s http://127.0.0.1:8930/api/trigger -X POST -H 'content-type: application/json' -d '{
  "source": {"type": "webhook"},
  "target": {"kind": "turn", "botId": "local_riff"},
  "envelope": {"format": "text", "sourceName": "my-runner", "trusted": false},
  "instruction": "Run the tests and report results",
  "options": {"asyncReturnSessionId": true}
}'
# → {"ok":true, "triggerId":"trg_...", "async":{"sessionId":"<uuid>", ...}}

# Poll: no signing
curl -s "http://127.0.0.1:8930/api/sessions/<uuid>/trigger-result"
# → state: running / completed / failed / not_found; an interrupted turn is interrupted

Use v3.9.0 or later. On older versions, a core-only claude-code first turn could stay running forever.

Stop just this turn (keep the session)

If a task goes off track and you want to stop it but keep the session for more turns, use the interrupt route (no signing):

curl -s -X POST "http://127.0.0.1:8930/api/sessions/<uuid>/turns/<triggerId>/interrupt"
# → {"ok":true, "action":"interrupted", "sessionId":"<uuid>", "triggerId":"trg_..."}

It only stops the turn you name. botmux first confirms the CLI is really running that turn before sending the interrupt; if it can't confirm, it refuses rather than stopping some other turn.

Polling that turn afterwards returns state: "interrupted". The session stays open, so you can send the next turn with target.sessionId.

Interrupting the same turn again just returns success (with idempotent: true).

Possible failures: 404 (session doesn't exist or is closed, or this session has no such turn), 409 (the turn already finished, isn't running in the current daemon process, or the CLI has already moved past it), 503 (the interrupt wasn't delivered; retry later).

To close the whole session, use POST /api/sessions/:id/close. It needs signing; see "Close the whole session" in Triggering Tasks via API.

Reading session-host facts

If you use botmux as a host for CLI sessions and need to know "is this session still there?", read:

curl -s "http://127.0.0.1:8930/api/sessions/<uuid>/host-facts"

It returns { ok: true, facts: {...} } with:

Field	Meaning
sessionId / cli / backend / sessionStatus	Session id, CLI, backend (tmux/pty), and whether the session is active or closed
liveness	One of exists / missing / unknown
worker.present / ready / generation	Whether a worker exists, whether it's ready, and which generation it is
native.sessionId	The CLI's own session/thread id
native.activeTurnId	botmux's id for the current turn (not the CLI's internal turn id)

It never returns a tmux socket, PID, worker token, environment variables, or terminal write access.

Two things to keep in mind:

unknown is not missing. Don't start a replacement session because of it.

A CLI turn ending doesn't mean your business task is done. Your orchestrator should still validate the result and save its own evidence before moving its state forward.

4. Web terminal

With a visible CLI (--cli codex, claude-code, etc.) you can watch the CLI live in a browser, or even type into it.

Read-only: already in the poll result

As long as the session's worker is alive, the trigger-result response also carries readOnlyUrl and viewToken. Open readOnlyUrl to watch; you can't type.

Once the session is closed, or after a restart before a live worker exists, these fields are left out, so any link you get can actually connect. This is core-only only; a normal fleet's poll response never carries them.

The viewToken belongs to the current worker: when the worker restarts it gets a new one and the old link stops working. Use the read-only link from your latest poll; don't cache it long-term.

Interactive: call write-link (signed)

# write-link needs the section 6 signature headers
curl -s "http://127.0.0.1:8930/api/sessions/<sid>/write-link" \
  -H "X-Botmux-Cli-Ts: ..." -H "X-Botmux-Cli-Nonce: ..." -H "X-Botmux-Cli-Auth: ..."
# → {"ok":true, "url":"http://127.0.0.1:<proxyPort>/s/<sid>?token=<write-token>"}

The URL carries a write token; opening it gives you a terminal you can type into. The write token is only available here and never appears in poll results.

Common errors: 401 (bad signature), 404 session_not_active (session not running), 409 terminal_unavailable (the worker terminal isn't available right now).

Fetch the URL each time you "open the terminal", and store only the sessionId. A session's write token stays the same across worker cycles and daemon restarts, but the port, host and whether the worker is online can change. Fetching is cheap (a local request plus a signature) and always gives you an address that connects.

A single core-only session isn't reclaimed for being idle (up to 30 live workers by default, and no idle timeout by default), so the terminal normally stays available.

5. Which routes need signing

Core-only routes come in three layers. Integrators only need the first; the other two help you understand the security boundary.

Layer 1: public routes (no signing) — only these:

Route	Method	Purpose
/healthz	GET	Readiness probe
/api/trigger	POST	Start a turn
/api/sessions/:id/trigger-result	GET	Poll the result
/api/sessions/:id/insight	GET	Poll conversation and progress
/api/sessions/:id/host-facts	GET	Read session-host facts
/api/sessions/:id/turns/:triggerId/interrupt	POST	Interrupt only the named turn

/__health is also public in every mode, but it only means the process is alive.

This list is deliberately narrow: other processes on the same machine (including commands the model itself runs) can reach 127.0.0.1 too, so only "drive your own task, read your own result" is open. For example /api/asks/answer, which answers an AskUserQuestion, is not on the list: it isn't tied to a session, so opening it would let another process answer on your behalf.

Layer 2: in-session routes (the CLI proves who it is). For example POST /api/session-ready, POST /api/asks, POST /api/sessions/:id/{slash,cd,close,…}, POST /api/hooks/emit. The caller is the CLI inside the session, using a per-turn rotating credential bound to its session, so it can only act on its own session. Integrators normally don't call these.

Layer 3: host / operator routes (need the section 6 signature). Everything not in the first two layers, e.g. GET /api/sessions/:id/write-link, GET /api/sessions/:id (session details), POST /api/sessions/:id/close.

close is a special case: external callers must sign, and the in-session CLI can also close itself with its layer-2 credential.

6. How to sign (the usual mistake is the bind)

Signed requests carry three headers:

Header	Value
X-Botmux-Cli-Ts	Unix timestamp in seconds; allowed skew ±30 seconds
X-Botmux-Cli-Nonce	Random hex string; must not repeat within 60 seconds
X-Botmux-Cli-Auth	HMAC_SHA256(secret, msg), encoded as base64url

secret is the 43-character base64url text in ~/.botmux/.dashboard-secret. Use it as-is as the key; don't base64-decode it first. The request must come from a loopback address.

msg must include the bind, which ties the signature to "method + path + port" so it can't be replayed against another route:

bind = `${METHOD} ${pathname} ${port}`     // e.g. "GET /api/sessions/<sid>/write-link 8930"
msg  = `${ts}:${nonce}:${bind}`

Three common mistakes:

port is the port the service actually listens on (e.g. 8930), not the value in the Host header.

pathname has no query string (use new URL(...).pathname).

secret is the raw string; don't decode it.

If you sign only ts:nonce and forget the bind, you get 401 {"reason":"sig_mismatch"}. Because public routes don't check signatures, this usually shows up the first time you call write-link, and it's easy to mistake for a wrong secret or clock. Other reason values: ts_window (clock off by more than 30 seconds), replay (repeated nonce), missing_headers.

Reference implementation (same logic as daemonIpcAuthHeaders() in src/core/daemon-ipc-auth.ts):

function coreOnlyAuthHeaders(secret, method, path, port) {
  const pathname = new URL(path, `http://127.0.0.1:${port}`).pathname; // strip the query string
  const ts = Math.floor(Date.now() / 1000).toString();
  const nonce = randomBytes(8).toString('hex');
  const bind = `${method.toUpperCase()} ${pathname} ${port}`;
  const sig = createHmac('sha256', secret)          // secret = raw base64url string
    .update(`${ts}:${nonce}:${bind}`)
    .digest('base64url');
  return {
    'X-Botmux-Cli-Ts': ts,
    'X-Botmux-Cli-Nonce': nonce,
    'X-Botmux-Cli-Auth': sig,
  };
}

7. Security boundary

Core-only doesn't talk to Feishu, serves a single tenant, and only uses loopback. Around that, it isolates itself by default:

No Feishu: never creates a Feishu client, and never hands larkAppSecret to CLI child processes.

No real bot config: ignores ~/.botmux/bots.json and removes BOTS_CONFIG from the environment, so the CLI can't read other bots' credentials on the same machine.

Separate data directory: session data always lives in ~/.botmux/core-only/<botId>/data (or your --state-dir). An inherited SESSION_DATA_DIR from a parent process can't point it at the real fleet's data. The internal signing key used for task reports also lives separately in this directory and is never shared with a fleet on the same machine. (The ~/.botmux/.dashboard-secret used for section 6 signatures is a different thing.)

Local only: the worker's web server and the advertised terminal address are both fixed to 127.0.0.1, never exposed on other interfaces.

Leaves the host install alone: no auto-update, auto-restart or botmux restart. The botmux command wrapper for the CLI goes into bin/ under its own data directory and never overwrites the machine's ~/.botmux/bin.

Loopback isn't trust: other processes on the machine (including sandboxes that share the network by default) can also reach 127.0.0.1, so every route outside layer 1 requires auth.

Appendix: route cheat-sheet

Route	Method	Auth	Purpose
/healthz	GET	public	Readiness probe (503 starting / 200 ok)
/api/trigger	POST	public	Start a turn (an HTTP response mode is required)
/api/sessions/:id/trigger-result	GET	public	Poll the result; carries readOnlyUrl + viewToken while the worker is alive
/api/sessions/:id/insight	GET	public	Poll conversation and progress
/api/sessions/:id/host-facts	GET	public	Session, CLI, backend and liveness
/api/sessions/:id/turns/:triggerId/interrupt	POST	public	Interrupt only the named turn; the session stays open
/api/sessions/:id/write-link	GET	signed	Interactive web terminal URL (fetch when opening)
/api/sessions/:id	GET	signed	Session details
/api/sessions/:id/close	POST	signed, or the in-session CLI's own credential	Close the session

For request fields, error codes, what each polling state means and restart behavior, see Triggering Tasks via API.
