title: Create a Session Group in One Step
content:
Want a clean group dedicated to one project or task? Send /group <group name> (short form /g). The bot will:

Create a new Lark group and add you to it;

Transfer group ownership to you;

Reply with a card containing the join link.

Open the group and start talking to the bot. The whole group is one independent CLI session (a session is one running AI coding CLI process, such as Claude Code or Codex).

/g card race-condition bug

The reply looks roughly like:

✅ Created group "card race-condition bug"
👉 <join link>

Just start chatting in the new group — the whole group is one CLI session.

Creating the group does not start a session. The session starts when you send your first message in the new group.

botmux has two kinds of "session group". This page covers both:

Groups created by /g	DM dedicated groups
How they appear	You send /g in any chat	Once enabled, every new DM to the bot creates its own group
Good for	Opening a workspace for a project / task by hand, optionally with several bots	Giving each DM question its own group so it is easy to look back on
See	"Create a group with /g" below	"DM dedicated groups" below

Create a group with /g

Group name and avatar

With a name: your name is used and never changed afterwards.

Without a name (just /g): the group starts with the placeholder "New session MM/DD HH:mm". After your first substantive message in it, the bot summarizes a title of up to 20 characters and renames the group.

Avatar: by default, the botmux logo on a gradient background (one of ten palettes, fixed per group). Add --avatar name for a text avatar showing the group name, or --avatar off to keep Lark's default.

A group-name text avatar generated by --avatar name

About automatic renaming:

Slash commands, messages that only contain images/attachments, and bot messages are not used for naming.

If you rename the group yourself first, your name wins.

In a multi-bot group, only the bot that created the group names it.

If naming fails, the placeholder stays and naming is retried on your next message (the two retries wait at least 30 seconds and 2 minutes), up to three rounds.

AI naming runs the CLI once on the host, so it only works when: the CLI is Claude Code, Codex, TRAE CLI (traex), OpenCode, Antigravity, Grok, Pi or oh-my-pi; the bot has no file sandbox; the host has no device-credential isolation; no custom launch mode is used; and Codex does not use private login or an instance pool. Otherwise the placeholder stays.

Bring several bots along

@-mention bots in the command and they are all added to the new group. The first @-mentioned bot creates it:

@Claude @Codex /g review group authorization

The reply lists "🤖 Bots in the group: Claude, Codex". In the group, @ whichever bot should do the work.

If you don't want to @ every time, use --agents with names or app IDs. The bots don't have to be in the current chat, but they must be configured in this machine's bots.json with a Lark connection:

/g Project work --agents Review,Build,Check

Names are case-insensitive. Unknown or duplicate names fail before the group is created; use app IDs for duplicates.

If you have set up a decision-board steward on this machine with "Add the steward to new chats" enabled, and the steward's owner is in the new group, the steward is added too (it stays silent and opens no session). Groups with only you and one bot don't get it by default.

All options

Option	Effect
--agents A,B	Also invite these bots (display names or app IDs, comma-separated); replaces the default list
--no-agents	Ignore the default invite list
--tag <name>	Put the new group into a message group in your Lark sidebar (up to 60 characters)
--no-tag	Ignore the default tag
--avatar logo|name|off	Avatar: gradient logo (default) / group-name text / Lark default
--role-profile <id>	Apply a role profile to the bots in the group after creation
--	End of options: everything after it is part of the group name, handy when the name itself contains text like --tag

/g Project work --agents Review,Build --tag Projects --avatar name
/g Project work --tag "Project work"
/g --avatar off

Notes:

Values can be written as --tag=Projects or --tag Projects; quote values with spaces.

Missing values, invalid values and repeated options fail before the group is created, so you never get a half-wrong group.

Unknown --xxx words are not errors; they stay in the group name as-is.

--tag is a message group in your personal sidebar, not a tenant-wide chat tag. The first time, authorize it: send /login tags in a chat with that bot and confirm the link. Without authorization the group is still created and the reply tells you what is missing.

Failures to invite bots, set the tag or set the avatar are reported separately in the reply; the created group is kept.

Apply a role profile

If you keep reusable collaboration personas in a role profile, add --role-profile when creating the group:

@Claude @Codex /g --role-profile collab-main review group authorization

After the group is created, the creator bot applies its own entry first, then posts @Codex /role profile apply collab-main --quiet in the new group so each other bot applies its own. A bot without an entry in the profile is fine; it keeps its default role.

Set defaults for a bot

If your team always uses the same set of bots and the same tag, give the bot defaults so a bare /g is enough. In that bot's bots.json entry:

{
  "groupCreation": {
    "agents": ["cli_review_app", "cli_build_app"],
    "tag": "Projects",
    "avatar": "name"
  }
}

You can also send /botconfig set groupCreation <JSON> in Lark, and /botconfig unset groupCreation to reset.

Options in the command override the defaults.

With a default list, @-mentioning just one of those bots with /g still brings in the whole team (deduplicated).

--no-agents, --no-tag and --avatar off only drop defaults; they never remove bots you explicitly @-mentioned.

Without groupCreation and without options, only the current bot and the bots you @-mentioned join.

Create a group in the Dashboard

Prefer not to type commands? Open the Group Management page in botmux dashboard and click "New Chat":

Check the bots to add (the Dashboard picks an online bot as the creator);

Enter a group name;

Optionally set "Bind Directory": new topics start the CLI there directly, without the repo picker;

Optionally choose a Lark tag (sidebar message group).

For an existing group, click "Duplicate": the source group's bots and bound directory are preselected, and you can also copy the per-group roles.

"Duplicate" (the screenshot shows the Chinese UI): bots and bound directory are preselected; per-group roles can be copied too

Click "Manage" on a group to open its details. The "Leave / Disband" tab lets selected bots leave the group, or disbands it. Disbanding only succeeds when a bot in the group is the owner; otherwise have the bots leave instead.

The "Leave / Disband" tab in group details (Chinese UI shown)

The top of the Group Management page switches between "Groups / Session chats"; session chats are sorted by recent activity by default, or by creation time. See Dashboard Control Panel for more.

DM dedicated groups

Once enabled, every new message you send the bot in a DM creates a group containing just you and that bot to host the conversation, and the DM gets a receipt with the group link.

Turn it on

Either:

Dashboard → Bot Config → Sessions → Session mode → for DMs choose "A dedicated group per message";

or send /botconfig set p2pMode group in Lark (/botconfig unset p2pMode goes back to the default "Continuous chat").

After /close, the group stays. A new message in it starts a fresh session; use /resume to continue the previous one.

How the group is named

Once DMs are set to "A dedicated group per message", a Dedicated group naming option appears below it. Choose there:

Option	Effect
AI summary (default)	Use a truncated first message as a placeholder, then generate a short title and rename
Reuse Agent session title	Use the title the CLI gives the session, with no extra model call; keep the placeholder until it's ready
Truncate first message	Use the truncated first message as the name and never rename

Or in that bot's bots.json:

{
  "sessionGroup": {
    "naming": { "mode": "session-title", "maxLen": 20 }
  }
}

mode is ai-summary / session-title / truncate; maxLen is the maximum title length (default 20).

Notes:

The group is named automatically once; later title changes are not followed, and a name you set by hand is never overwritten.

"Reuse Agent session title" accepts Codex's own session titles and titles published through botmux renames (including Agent renames and renames you make in the Dashboard or inside a session).

For AI summaries, Codex uses an isolated lightweight call: low reasoning, none of your hooks, plugins, MCP servers or project instructions, only the login credentials and model gateway settings. Enter a lightweight model your account can use in "Summary model (Codex)" (naming.model in bots.json), or leave it blank to use the bot's model. This only affects group naming, not conversations.

Change the tag on close

By default, dedicated groups go into a message group in your sidebar (such as "XX sessions"). To move closed sessions into another message group automatically (for example "Closed"), set Tag after closing under Dashboard "Bot Config → Sessions → Session mode → Direct messages" (shown once DMs are set to "A dedicated group per message"). Leave it empty to disable.

Equivalent bots.json:

{
  "p2pMode": "group",
  "sessionGroup": {
    "tag": {
      "mode": "feed-group",
      "name": "Active",
      "closedName": "Closed"
    }
  }
}

Rules:

The move only happens after a successful /close (or the close-card button). /stop, failed closes, crashes and background cleanup never trigger it.

The group is added to the new message group first, then removed from the old one. A missing message group is created; one with the same name is reused. The group and its history are untouched.

Only personal message groups (feed-group) are supported, using the group creator's authorization; send /login tags if it's missing.

The move runs in the background; failures are reported separately.

Resuming a session does not move the group back. Clearing "Tag after closing" turns the feature off without bulk-migrating existing groups.

Disband a dedicated group: /dismiss

Want to delete the whole group? Send /dismiss at the top level of the dedicated group. The bot replies with a confirmation card listing:

The sessions in this group that will be closed (including other local bots' sessions in this group);

Disbanding this Lark group (it disappears for all members; cannot be undone);

Removing the session-group record (resuming these sessions later will not recreate the group).

Click "Disband" to proceed. On success the group disappears and you get the result as a private card. The card also lists the worktrees those sessions used, with a one-click cleanup (equivalent to git worktree remove --force: uncommitted changes are lost, branches and committed work stay). If you don't click it, they are kept.

Limits and notes:

Only the person who created the group, with bot operator permission, can run it.

The bot must own the group, or be its creator with the im:chat:operate_as_owner permission.

In a dedicated group it only works at the top level, not in subtopics. DMs are not supported. For ordinary groups, see below.

It stops without disbanding, and explains why in the group, when: the group has a shared session attached via /adopt (run /detach first), another local bot is offline, a session couldn't be closed safely, or a new session appeared during confirmation.

If disbanding fails, sessions that were closed stay closed; send /dismiss again to retry.

Code and worktrees are not deleted by default. To end the session but keep the group, use /close.

Ordinary and topic groups

Groups that were not opened from a DM (ordinary and topic groups) also accept /dismiss, from any topic, when both hold:

The sender has bot operator permission;

The bot owns the group and is the only bot in it. Lark cannot confirm in advance whether a disband would succeed otherwise, so the bot replies that it has no permission and closes no session.

The confirmation card lists every session this machine's bots hold in the group (every topic's session in a topic group) and states that the whole group is disbanded for everyone in it. After you confirm, those sessions are closed first, and the group is disbanded only once all of them are closed; the result arrives as a private card. It stops in the same cases as above.

title: Headless Automation Sessions
content:
botmux session lets scripts, CI jobs, or scheduled jobs start an AI session without a Feishu group: send a prompt, wait for it to finish, and read the result. When people need to see it, one command publishes the session to a new group or binds it to an existing group / topic, and the conversation continues in Feishu.

Good fits:

In CI, let the AI review code first, and only open a group to notify people when something is wrong;

Run batch analysis from a script when you only want the text result and no chat noise;

Do the investigation in the background, then hand the team "the existing context + a summary" in one go.

How the two command sets relate: botmux session is the stable, automation-facing entry point; botmux headless is the layer underneath. Prefer session in scripts. Use headless when you need finer control (for example, post one turn's result without moving the session).

Three steps

Prerequisite: the botmux daemon is running on this machine (botmux start).

# 1. Start a session, run the first turn, and wait for it
botmux session start --headless --bot <bot-name> --working-dir ~/repo \
  --prompt-file task.md --json > start.json
SID=$(jq -r .sessionId start.json)       # session ID, starts with hl_
jq -r '.output.content' start.json       # reply to the first turn

# 2. Optionally ask follow-ups, or fetch the result again
botmux session send "$SID" --prompt-file followup.md --wait --json
botmux session result "$SID" --json

# 3. Hand it to people: create a group and publish the session there
botmux session publish "$SID" --create-group --name "Dependency upgrade check"

Step 3 does three things:

Creates a new Feishu group with this bot (with --chat-id it uses an existing group instead);

Opens a topic in the group and moves the session into it;

Asks the AI to summarize the context so far (what was done, key findings and evidence, open questions, suggested next steps), then posts the summary in the topic.

From then on, replying in that topic talks to the same session with the same memory.

Session IDs

Starting a session gives you two IDs; commands accept either:

ID	Looks like	Notes
Session ID (sessionId / headlessId)	starts with hl_	Save this one in scripts
botmux session ID (botmuxSessionId)	UUID	Same ID you see in botmux ls and other commands

botmux headless subcommands also accept an ID prefix (it must match uniquely); session publish needs the full ID.

session commands at a glance

I want to…	Command
Start a session and run the first turn	botmux session start --headless --bot <bot> [--working-dir <dir>] --prompt-file <path>
Send another turn to a session	botmux session send <id> --prompt-file <path> [--wait]
Wait for the current turn to finish	botmux session wait <id> [--trigger-id <triggerId>]
Check the result now (no waiting)	botmux session result <id> [--trigger-id <triggerId>]
List headless sessions on this machine	botmux session list [--bot <larkAppId>]
Bind to an existing group / topic	botmux session bind <id> --chat-id <oc_xxx> [--into <om_xxx>]
Summarize and publish to a new group	botmux session publish <id> --create-group --name "Task name"
Summarize and publish to an existing group	botmux session publish <id> --chat-id <oc_xxx> [--name "Topic title"]
Model-only structured call	botmux session invoke <start|result|cancel|capabilities> --bot <larkAppId>, see below

Every command supports --json, which prints JSON that is easy to parse with jq. Without it you get compact text:

start: the first line is the session ID, followed by the reply;

send --wait / wait / result: the reply when finished, otherwise the state (such as running);

publish: the first line is the group ID, the second is the triggerId of the summary turn.

send / wait / result / list / bind (and create / run) are passed straight through to the matching botmux headless subcommand with the same arguments.

Common options

Option	Used by	Notes
--bot	start	Bot name or larkAppId. Optional when only one daemon is online on this machine; required when there are several
--working-dir	start	Working directory for the session. Defaults to the bot's default directory, then the daemon's current directory
--prompt-file / --prompt	start / send	Where the prompt comes from, pick one; with neither, it is read from stdin. --prompt-file - also means stdin
--model	start	Model for this session
--reasoning-effort	start	Reasoning effort: low / medium / high / xhigh / max / ultra
--timeout	start / send / wait	Maximum seconds the command waits, 1–86400, default 300
--name	start / publish	In start, the session title; in publish --create-group, the group name (required), also used as the topic title
--trigger-id	wait / result	A specific turn; defaults to the latest one
--json	all	Print JSON

--timeout only controls how long the command waits. When it runs out, the command exits normally while the AI keeps working; fetch the result later with session wait or session result. With --json, a timed-out result includes "timedOut": true and the state is still running.

Result states (state):

State	Meaning
running	Still running
completed	Done; the reply is in output.content
failed	Failed
interrupted	Interrupted
not_found	No such session or turn

Exit codes: non-zero when the state is failed or not_found; 2 for invalid arguments.

When session start fails (non-zero exit), it prints the raw JSON from the underlying headless run, not the compact format above; the session ID is in created.headlessId.

Publish and bind: hand it to people

I want to…	Use	Where the session goes	What the group sees
Hand it to the team with a summary first	session publish	Moved into a new topic	Topic title + a fresh summary from the AI
Move it into an existing topic	session bind --into <om_xxx>	Moved into that topic	The latest reply
Move it into an existing group as a new topic	session bind --chat-id <oc_xxx>	Moved into a new topic (titled with the session title)	The latest reply
Post one turn's result without moving the session	headless publish	Stays in the background	That turn's reply

Notes:

The bot must be in the target group, or the post fails. With --create-group, the bot creates the group itself and invites the first user in that bot's allowedUsers.

A group made by --create-group is bound to the session's working directory, so new topics in that group start there too.

To change what the summary asks for, publish accepts --summary-prompt "<text>" or --summary-prompt-file <path> to replace the default summary prompt.

The session must be idle to be moved. If the AI is in the middle of a turn, the move is refused; try again after the turn ends.

What moves is the same CLI process and the same memory — the same mechanism as Session Relay.

bind re-posts the latest reply into the group by default. In that case the latest turn must be finished and have a reply, or the bind is refused; add --replay none to skip the re-post.

botmux headless: the lower layer

Use it directly when you need finer control.

Subcommand	What it does
create	Create a session without sending a prompt. Accepts --bot --title --working-dir --model --reasoning-effort
run	Send one turn. Without --session it creates a session first; it only waits with --wait
send --session <id>	Send a turn to an existing session (the ID can also be the first argument)
wait <id>	Wait for a turn to finish, 300 seconds max by default
result <id>	Check a turn's result now
list / ls	List sessions; filter with --bot <larkAppId>
publish <id>	Post one turn's result as text to a group: --chat-id picks the group (defaults to the bound group), --into <om_xxx> replies in a topic
bind <id> --chat-id <oc_xxx>	Move the session into a group, see below

bind options:

Option	Default	Notes
--scope thread|chat	thread	thread: a topic session; chat: the whole group is the session
--into <om_xxx>	none	Bind to the topic this message belongs to. Without it, a title message is posted to start a new topic. Required with --scope chat (as an anchor message)
--title	session title	Title of the new topic
--replay latest|none	latest	Whether to post the latest reply (or the turn given by --trigger-id) into the group

session start is equivalent to headless run --wait --json, with the output reshaped into a shorter JSON (sessionId, triggerId, state, output; the full raw response is in raw).

session invoke: model-only structured calls

This is a different mode: no agent loop, no tools at all — the model just returns a structured result that matches your JSON Schema. Good for "ask once, get JSON" tasks such as classification or extraction.

botmux session invoke capabilities --bot <larkAppId>      # check whether this bot supports it
botmux session invoke start  --bot <larkAppId> --request-file req.json --wait-ms 60000
botmux session invoke result --bot <larkAppId> --request-id job-001 --wait-ms 30000
botmux session invoke cancel --bot <larkAppId> --request-id job-001

Example req.json:

{
  "requestId": "job-001",
  "prompt": "Is this log a network timeout? ...",
  "model": "<model-name>",
  "deadlineMs": 60000,
  "outputSchema": {
    "type": "object",
    "properties": { "timeout": { "type": "boolean" }, "reason": { "type": "string" } },
    "required": ["timeout", "reason"],
    "additionalProperties": false
  }
}

Key points:

--bot must be the larkAppId here.

The requirements are strict: the bot must be a dedicated Core-only bot without sandbox, extra env vars, and so on; only some CLIs support it so far (Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Pi, and a few others). The supported field from capabilities is the source of truth.

deadlineMs (100–300000) actually stops inference when reached; --wait-ms (up to 300000) only controls how long the command waits.

The schema supports a small set of keywords (type properties required additionalProperties items enum description); objects must list every property in required and set additionalProperties: false.

Output is always one line of JSON. Exit code is 0 when the state is running or completed, otherwise 1.

FAQ

I get no online botmux daemon or daemon not online for bot ....
The daemon for that bot isn't running. Run botmux start, then check with botmux status.

I get multiple daemons online; pass --bot.
Several bots run on this machine; pick one with --bot on start.

Does the session post anything in Feishu?
No. Until it is published or bound, the session has no group: no cards, no messages, results are only available through the commands. These turns are also outside what the Turn Results API collects.

How does this relate to HTTP triggers?
Under the hood, botmux headless sends the local daemon a task request with source.type set to headless. To call the HTTP API directly, see Trigger botmux Tasks via API.

publish failed. Is the session still there?
Yes. publish runs "create group → bind → summarize → post the summary" in order and stops with an error at the step that fails. If binding already succeeded, the session is already in the group's topic; just continue there.

Related

Session Relay: move sessions between groups, topics, and DMs

Trigger botmux Tasks via API: start tasks and fetch results over HTTP

Core-only (apiOnly) API Control: botmux with only the HTTP API, no Feishu

CLI Commands

toc.text: Publish and bind: hand it to people

description: botmux session lets scripts, CI jobs, or scheduled jobs start an AI session without a Feishu group: send a prompt, wait for it to finish, and read the result. When people need to see it, one command publishes the session to a new group or binds it to an existing group / topic, and the conversation continues in Feishu. Good fits: In CI, let the AI review code first, and only open a group to notify people when something is wrong;Run batch analysis from a script when you only want the text result and no chat noise;Do the investigation in the background, then hand the team "the existing context + a summary" in one go. How the two command sets relate: botmux session is the stable, automation-facing entry point; botmux headless is the layer underneath. Prefer session in scripts. Use headless when you need finer control (for example, post one turn's result without moving the session).

title: Lifecycle Hooks
content:
Hooks let botmux run your own command at key moments: a new topic arrives, a session starts or exits, something needs a human, a turn finishes… Use them to send notifications, keep audit logs, auto-update skills, or run a custom check before a message reaches the CLI.

There are two kinds of hooks:

Kind	How to write it	Does botmux wait?	Good for
Notification (default)	Omit mode, or "mode": "async"	No. Failures, timeouts, or a missing command only go to the log and never affect messaging	Push notifications, auditing, metrics, kicking off external flows
Gate	"mode": "sync", only on prompt.submit and chat.bot_added	Yes, it waits for "allow / deny"	Permission or content checks before a message reaches the CLI; deciding whether to auto-start after joining a group

5-minute start: log events to a local file

Write a minimal hook script that appends the incoming JSON to a log:

mkdir -p ~/bin
cat > ~/bin/botmux-hook-log.sh <<'SH'
#!/bin/bash
{ echo "== $BOTMUX_HOOK_EVENT $(date)"; cat; echo; } >> /tmp/botmux-hook.log
SH
chmod +x ~/bin/botmux-hook-log.sh

Write the config file ~/.botmux/data/hooks.json (prefer an absolute path for command: the hook gets the daemon's PATH, which may differ from your terminal's):

mkdir -p ~/.botmux/data
cat > ~/.botmux/data/hooks.json <<JSON
[
  { "event": "session.start", "command": "$HOME/bin/botmux-hook-log.sh" },
  { "event": "turn.finished", "command": "$HOME/bin/botmux-hook-log.sh" }
]
JSON

Send a message in Feishu, then watch the log:

tail -f /tmp/botmux-hook.log

Editing hooks.json does not require a daemon restart: botmux checks the file whenever an event fires and reloads it when it changes.

The source repo's examples/hooks/ has ready-made examples: echo-to-log.sh (log), osascript-notify.sh (macOS Notification Center), http-webhook.sh (forward to an HTTP endpoint), prompt-gate.sh (sync gate). The npm package does not include this directory; copy them from the GitHub repo if you need them.

Where the config lives

From highest to lowest precedence; only the first one found is used:

Env var BOTMUX_HOOKS_JSON: a JSON array inline

Env var BOTMUX_HOOKS_FILE: path to a JSON file

Default file ~/.botmux/data/hooks.json (or hooks.json under SESSION_DATA_DIR if that is set)

The content is an array; each item is one hook. You can attach several hooks to the same event. If the JSON fails to parse, none of it takes effect and the log shows [hooks] Failed to load hook config.

Config fields

[
  {
    "event": "session.requires_attention",
    "command": "/absolute/path/to/your-hook --flag value",
    "timeoutMs": 5000,
    "filter": { "chatId": "oc_xxx" },
    "redact": { "fullContentEvents": ["session.requires_attention"] }
  }
]

Field	Required	Description
event	Yes	Event to subscribe to; see "Events" below. Entries with an unknown event are ignored
command	Yes	Command to run, with arguments (quotes supported). No shell; see "Execution environment" below
timeoutMs	No	Timeout in ms, default 5000. On timeout botmux sends SIGTERM, then SIGKILL, to the whole process group
mode	No	async (default, notification) or sync (gate). sync only works on prompt.submit and chat.bot_added; on other events it is treated as async with a warning in the log
onError	No	Only for sync: what to do when the hook itself breaks (timeout, command not found, crash). Default allow; can be deny
filter.larkAppId	No	Only for one (or several) Bot apps. String or array
filter.chatId	No	Only for one (or several) chats. String or array
filter.senderOpenId	No	Only for one (or several) senders. Events without a sender (such as session.start) never match
redact.fullContentEvents	No	Long text is truncated by default; events listed here get full text for this hook

All conditions in filter must match together; an array inside one condition means "any of these". If the event lacks the field, that condition does not match.

Events

Event	When it fires	Extra fields
topic.new	A new topic or new @mention arrives	messageId, senderOpenId, senderType, msgType, content
thread.reply	A reply arrives in an existing topic	messageId, rootId, parentId, senderOpenId, senderType, msgType, sessionId, content
prompt.submit	A message has passed the built-in permission checks and is about to be handed to the CLI. Works as a notification or a gate	messageId, senderOpenId, senderUnionId, memberUnionId, botSender, talkReason, content, attachments
outbound.send	After botmux sends a regular message	messageId, msgType, uuid, content
outbound.reply	After botmux replies in a topic	messageId, replyId, msgType, replyInThread, uuid, content
schedule.fired	A scheduled-task check and submit has finished (ok, skipped, or error)	id, name, schedule, status, error, rootMessageId, runAt; multi-chat tasks also carry chatIds
session.start	A session process started (including resume and adopt)	reason, pid; adopt also has adoptedFrom
session.exit	A session process exited, crashed, or the session was closed	reason, code
session.idle	A session enters or leaves idle	prevState, newState, transition (enter / exit), source, content (screen text at the time)
session.requires_attention	Something needs a human (reason values below)	reason, plus message, kind, errorCode, turnId / logicalTurnId, etc. depending on the case
turn.finished	A turn ended (success, failure, or cancel)	turnId, status, terminalStatus, senderOpenId, dispatchAttempt
chat.bot_added	The Bot was added to a group (subscribe to im.chat.member.bot.added_v1 in the Feishu console)	operatorOpenId (who added the Bot); the sync gate also gets chatName, chatDescription, chatMode, chatFetchStatus

Fields on every event

The payload is written as JSON to the command's stdin, and the env var BOTMUX_HOOK_EVENT=<event name> is set.

Every payload has event and emittedAt (ISO time).

Most events also carry larkAppId and chatId; session events (session.*) also carry sessionId, chatType, scope, anchor, title, cliId, workingDir, hasHistory, spawnedAt, lastMessageAt.

Long text is truncated

content, message, description, finalOutput, and lastScreenContent are truncated past 600 characters. These fields always come with xxxLength (original length) and xxxTruncated (whether it was cut). For full text, list the event in this hook's redact.fullContentEvents. Sync gates are the exception and always get full text (see below).

Event details

session.exit: reason is graceful (exit code 0), exit_code_<N>, or dashboard_close (the session was closed on purpose, e.g. from the Dashboard; there is no code field). Not emitted when the daemon itself shuts down.

session.idle: fires at most once per session per state within 10 seconds, so flapping doesn't flood you.

schedule.fired: status matches the task's "last status":

status	Meaning
ok	Handed to the executor. It does not mean the model finished or the message was delivered
error	Pre-check or submit failed; the reason is in error
skipped	Pre-conditions not met; the model was not called

A skip doesn't use up a repeat and doesn't delete the task. A skipped one-shot task stays enabled and is rechecked after at least 30 seconds; recurring tasks continue on their normal schedule. If your script only handles ok / error, add a skipped branch and don't treat it as success.

turn.finished:

status is the simplified result, success or error; terminalStatus is the raw result, completed, failed, cancelled, or ambiguous (use it to tell cancel from failure).

senderOpenId is who started this turn; if unknown, the field is omitted rather than filled with the session owner.

Each turn (per dispatch attempt) fires once per daemon process; after a daemon restart it may fire again, so dedupe on sessionId + turnId + dispatchAttempt. A retried turn has a different dispatchAttempt, and each attempt fires.

If the session process exits without finishing a turn, no turn.finished is sent for it (the exit goes through session.exit).

It only says "this turn ended" and carries no duration or usage. For those, use the turn.completed outbound event in the Bot's feedbackWebhooks config.

The same notification also appears on the daemon's local GET /api/events stream.

Meeting (VC) receiver sessions never trigger session.* or turn.finished hooks, because they process external meeting content.

reason values for session.requires_attention

reason	Situation
user_notify	The session process raised something you need to handle, e.g. input could not be submitted to the CLI
agent_request	The agent raised its hand with botmux send --attention; kind is authz / decision / blocked / help, message is the reason
stuck_warning	The session looks stuck on some screen; also has elapsedMs, matchedPattern
worker_start_failed, worker_fork_error	The session process failed to start
ordinary_turn_recovery_exhausted	A turn failed and automatic retries ran out
task_continuation_stopped	Automatic continuation stopped
claude_terminal_failure_unrecovered	A turn failed (CLI error or it exited mid-turn) and could not recover automatically. The "claude" in the name is historical; other CLIs send it too
card_content_rejected, content_audit_blocked	Feishu rejected the final reply (card format or content audit)
topic_send_blocked	The original topic is no longer available and sending stopped (see Stop sending when the topic is unavailable)

New reason values may be added later; give unknown values a default branch in your script.

Outbound events can't block anything

outbound.send / outbound.reply fire after Feishu has accepted the message, so it's already in the chat. They don't support sync and are notifications only.

Sync gate: run your check before a message reaches the CLI

Add a "mode": "sync" hook on prompt.submit and every message headed for the CLI asks it first: allow or deny.

[
  {
    "event": "prompt.submit",
    "mode": "sync",
    "command": "/root/bin/prompt-gate.sh",
    "timeoutMs": 3000,
    "onError": "allow"
  }
]

examples/hooks/prompt-gate.sh in the source repo is a good starting point.

How to answer "allow / deny"

Either way works; JSON on stdout wins:

Method	How	Notes
JSON (recommended)	Print {"decision":"deny","reason":"why"} to stdout	decision is allow or deny; reason is shown to the user (up to 300 chars)
Exit code	Print no JSON, just exit 0 or exit 1	0 allows, non-zero denies; stderr becomes the reason

stdout must be entirely one JSON object to count. A few log lines on stdout fall back to the exit code.

When denied, the user gets "🚫 This message was blocked by a pre-submit check and was not sent to the CLI" in the topic, followed by the reason.

When it runs

Feishu message → built-in permission check → 🚦 prompt.submit gate → charge quota → download attachments
              → create/wake session → type text into CLI + Enter → CLI starts working

The gate runs in the daemon, before the CLI has seen this message (for a new topic the CLI hasn't even started). A denied message never reaches the CLI at all.

Note: there is no "text already typed in the CLI input box, before Enter" moment. botmux types the text and presses Enter in one step, with nowhere to insert a check.

Rules at a glance

You want to know	What happens
Can it loosen permissions?	No. Built-in checks (allowedUsers, grants, oncall, quota) run first; the hook is only asked if they all pass. An allow can't let in someone they rejected
Does a deny cost quota?	No, the gate runs before quota is charged
Several sync hooks	All must allow; hooks after the first deny don't run
The hook itself breaks	onError applies, default allow. For "deny everything if the checker is down", set "onError": "deny"; the user then sees the reason permission check failed
timeoutMs: 0	⚠️ Not "no limit" but "time out instantly", which means the gate does nothing (default allow). A warning is logged on load. Use a real budget like 3000
Does it slow things down?	Yes, gate time is added directly to message intake. Aim for 1–3 s. A slow gate makes later messages in the same topic queue up and may make this Bot's Dashboard actions (closing sessions, editing config) time out. No sync hook means zero overhead
How much text does it see?	Full text, never truncated (otherwise padding past 600 chars would bypass it). ⚠️ So configuring a gate hands the full message to that command
Can it see attachments?	Only metadata, attachments: [{type, name}], e.g. [{"type":"file","name":"prod.env"}], enough for "no .env uploads" or "images only"; not the file contents (attachments aren't downloaded yet)
Which messages go through it	New topics, topic replies, slash commands that start a session, the first message in a session group, external content matched by a message listener (denials there are only logged, no reply). Saved workflows also pass the gate, but without the text, so only sender-based rules apply
Which don't	Prompts sent automatically by scheduled tasks (automation you configured yourself); control messages that never reach the CLI
Will it run twice?	No. A config entry that runs as a gate isn't run again as a notification

Notify and gate on the same event

prompt.submit can also be a plain notification (no mode). Both can coexist:

[
  { "event": "prompt.submit", "command": "/root/bin/audit-log.sh" },
  { "event": "prompt.submit", "mode": "sync", "command": "/root/bin/prompt-gate.sh", "timeoutMs": 3000 }
]

Notifications are sent before the verdict, so they see denied messages too, which is exactly what an audit of "whose message got blocked" needs.

Notification hooks get text truncated to 600 chars as usual; only the gate gets full text.

A notification hook's exit code and output never affect the verdict.

Try it

cat > /tmp/gate.sh <<'SH'
#!/bin/bash
cat > /tmp/gate-payload.json
echo '{"decision":"deny","reason":"gate test: not allowed yet"}'
SH
chmod +x /tmp/gate.sh

cat > ~/.botmux/data/hooks.json <<'JSON'
[{ "event": "prompt.submit", "mode": "sync", "command": "/tmp/gate.sh", "timeoutMs": 3000 }]
JSON

Send the Bot a message in Feishu. You should get the "blocked by a pre-submit check" reply, and /tmp/gate-payload.json will hold the payload. Restore hooks.json when you're done.

Join gate: decide whether to auto-start after being added to a group

If the Bot has join auto-start on (autoStartOnGroupJoin, see bots.json), you can add a sync hook on chat.bot_added to decide per group. The hook sees the group name chatName, description chatDescription, group type chatMode, and who added the Bot, operatorOpenId.

[
  {
    "event": "chat.bot_added",
    "mode": "sync",
    "command": "/root/bin/join-gate.sh",
    "timeoutMs": 3000,
    "onError": "deny",
    "filter": { "larkAppId": "cli_xxx" }
  }
]

Key points:

It decides only join auto-start. Async chat.bot_added notifications and groupJoinCommand (run a command on join) keep running regardless.

Scope it with filter.larkAppId / filter.chatId. Don't use filter.senderOpenId: join events have no sender, so it never matches. To decide by inviter, read operatorOpenId in your script.

For "do nothing at all unless it's a target group": set autoStartOnGroupJoinGateRequired: true on the Bot and give the gate "onError": "deny". Then a missing, unmatched, timed-out, or crashed gate means no auto-start, instead of auto-starting in every new group.

With autoStartOnGroupJoinGateRequired: true, the first-turn prompt also includes a group-join block and the inviter; without it, the first-turn prompt is exactly as before.

This join info only shows "the Bot was added to this group". It does not prove the first-turn caller is an authenticated human, so the first turn doesn't get human-only privileges (such as auto-continuation or creating scheduled tasks directly). If the inviter is an app or bot, it isn't recorded as the session owner either.

Manual force-start entry points skip this gate.

To give one Bot its own join script (runs directly, no model), groupJoinCommand in bots.json is simpler; edit it in the Dashboard under Bot Config → Proactive Start. Its timeout is 10 minutes.

Execution environment

Before writing your own hook, know how it runs:

Any executable works: bash, Python, Node, a Go binary, an internal CLI, an HTTP forwarder.

No shell: command is just split on spaces and quotes into program + arguments. Pipes |, redirects >, &&, and ~ expansion don't work. Use a script, or bash -c '…'.

Minimal env vars: only basics such as PATH, HOME, TMPDIR, SHELL, USER, LANG, plus BOTMUX_HOOK_EVENT. App secrets and API keys are not passed. export anything else you need inside your script.

Payload on stdin: one JSON object. It's fine not to read it.

Timeouts kill the whole process group, including child processes your script started.

Nobody reads notification output: non-zero exit, timeout, or command not found only go to the botmux log and never affect messaging, scheduled tasks, or sessions.

Recipe: auto-update Skills when a session starts

botmux has built-in skill management (botmux skills install … to install, botmux skills update <name> to update, botmux skills list to list installed ones). With session.start you can check for updates every time a new session starts, similar to Claude Code's SessionStart hook.

Update one skill:

[
  { "event": "session.start", "command": "botmux skills update my-skill-name", "timeoutMs": 60000 }
]

Update all installed skills: botmux skills update takes a single name (no *), so loop in a script:

#!/bin/bash
# ~/bin/botmux-update-all-skills.sh
botmux skills list | cut -f1 | while read -r name; do
  [ -n "$name" ] && botmux skills update "$name"
done

[
  { "event": "session.start", "command": "/root/bin/botmux-update-all-skills.sh", "timeoutMs": 120000 }
]

Call agentbuddy directly to update user-global skills: hooks run without a shell and with a trimmed environment, so use a wrapper script:

#!/bin/bash
# ~/bin/agentbuddy-update.sh
export npm_config_registry="https://your-registry.example.com"  # if you use a private npm registry
npx -y agentbuddy update -y 2>/dev/null

[
  { "event": "session.start", "command": "/root/bin/agentbuddy-update.sh", "timeoutMs": 120000 }
]

Notes:

Raise timeoutMs: the 5 s default is rarely enough for a network update; use 60 s or more.

Doesn't block the session: updates run in the background and the current session doesn't wait; results take effect in the next new session.

Narrow the scope: use filter.chatId / filter.larkAppId to run only for certain chats or Bots.

Prefer botmux skills update: it updates the botmux-managed skill version, stays in step with botmux's skill lifecycle, and for skills installed from agentbuddy it strips the embedded usage telemetry.

title: botmux
content:
botmux is a bridge. It runs a background service (the daemon) on your dev machine that listens to Lark messages:

Each new topic gets its own AI coding CLI (30+ supported, including Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, OpenCode, and Antigravity)

Every turn of CLI output is streamed live into a Lark streaming card

When you want to take over, a card button opens the Web Terminal, so you can drive the same CLI from a browser or phone

Whether you're on your phone, at your desk, or in a terminal, you're looking at the same session.

5-minute start

curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/deepcoldy/botmux/master/install.sh | sh
botmux setup     # scan a QR code to create the Lark app → pick a CLI → pick a working directory (permissions and release are configured for you)
botmux start     # start the daemon; run botmux autostart enable to start on boot

Then DM the bot, or open the management page with botmux dashboard and create a group to start chatting.

What you install is a self-contained single-file binary that doesn't need Node on the machine. It supports Linux / macOS (x64 / arm64); on Windows, use WSL2

Prefer npm? npm i -g botmux works too and ships the same binary

On a Mac you can also install the macOS Desktop App to start and stop the service, open the Dashboard, and read logs with a click

To upgrade later: botmux update, or rerun the curl command above (releases older than v3.18.0: curl only), then botmux restart

For the full walkthrough (Lark international, manual permission setup, troubleshooting), see Quick start.

What problems it solves

Your pain	What botmux does
The CLI runs on your dev machine, so you can't see or steer it when you're away	Each turn is pushed to a Lark card; check, follow up, or interrupt from your phone, and open the Web Terminal when you need hands-on control
The CLI has no idea what's happening in Lark	Add the bot to a group and @ it to start working in your local codebase; /relay moves a running session (same CLI process, same AI memory) to another group so you can keep going there
One agent isn't enough	Put several bots backed by different CLIs in one group and @ whoever should do the work, e.g. have Claude Code and Codex review the same change

Common features

I want to...	See
Understand the live-updating card and its buttons	Streaming cards
Drive the CLI from a browser or phone	Web Terminal
Have several bots in one group split the work	Multi-bot collaboration
Split a big task into parallel topics	Multi-topic orchestration
Pin a card in the group that tracks a project's goal, to-dos, and sub-tasks	Project Progress Card
Hand dev tasks to a steward and collect everything you need to decide in one place	Decision Board and Steward
Bring a CLI already running in a local terminal into Lark	Session adopt (/adopt)
Move a session to another group	Session relay (/relay)
Run tasks on a schedule (alert analysis, group digests, etc.)	Scheduled tasks
Trigger tasks from an external system	Webhook · API task trigger
Run sessions from scripts or CI without a Lark group	Headless Automation Sessions
Ask the AI directly in Lark doc comments	Doc comment watching
Let anyone in an on-call group @ the bot for answers	On-Call Mode
Switch CLIs, or pick a CLI for one session	CLI adapters
Manage bots, sessions, and config in a web UI	Dashboard · Global Settings
Watch several sessions' progress and terminals at once	Agent Workbench
Manage several machines in one website, open Dashboards and terminals from anywhere, and work with a team	Central Platform (open source)

More: Roles & teams · File sandbox · Voice summary · Local whiteboard · Persistent tmux sessions · Feedback storage · Model Proxy (experimental) · Slash commands · CLI commands · Architecture overview · Best practices

Design philosophy: bridge the CLI, don't rebuild the agent

botmux does not reimplement agent capabilities. Memory, context management, tool calls, permissions, plan mode, / commands, and MCP are left to the CLI itself. When a CLI upgrades, most new capabilities just work in botmux (only when a CLI changes its flags, output format, or resume behavior does the matching adapter need an update).

Just write in plain language. The daemon wraps your message and the system instructions separately in a structured format (XML tags) before handing them to the CLI, so you never have to write any special format yourself.

Compared with approaches "rebuilt on top of an Agent SDK", the difference is mainly in how things are integrated:

Aspect	botmux	Agent SDK-based approach
What gets bridged	The full CLI process, with its own hooks / memory / plan mode / MCP / / commands	Whatever the SDK exposes
CLI upgrades	Most capabilities benefit directly	Depends on the SDK version and your integration
Memory / context	Uses the CLI's built-in memory	Depends on the SDK or your own build
Multiple CLIs	30+ adapters, switch with one config change	Depends on SDK coverage
Multiple bots	Several bots in one group, dispatched by @	Depends on implementation
Direct terminal access	With the tmux backend, tmux attach into the real CLI process	Depends on implementation

➡️ Next: Quick start

Project: https://github.com/deepcoldy/botmux

title: Mention Policy (`mention-mode`)
content:
In a regular group, the bot by default answers only messages that explicitly @-mention it. The mention policy decides when you can skip the @.

It only decides "is this message calling this bot?" — it does not grant permissions. Skipping the @ never skips authorization: people without talk access are still blocked (see Permissions & Authorization).

Pick a mode

Mode	Name in the Dashboard	What it does	Good for
always (default)	Require @	Answers only when @-mentioned	Large groups; quietest
topic	No @ inside topics	Top-level messages still need @; replies inside a topic this bot already handles don't	Follow-up questions in topics
never	No @ anywhere	Answers anything from people with talk access, including non-@ top-level messages (which directly create or resume a session)	Dedicated groups, on-call groups
ambient	No @, yield	No @ needed, like never — but if a message @-mentions another member (person or bot) and not this bot, the bot stays silent, because someone else was called	The "default responder" in multi-bot / multi-person groups

Two more notes:

@all does not count as calling someone else; under ambient the bot still answers.

Under topic, a reply inside a topic that only @-mentions someone else also makes the bot yield.

How to set it

There are two levels, and the per-group setting wins:

Level	Scope	Where to change it
Bot default	Every regular group this bot is in	Dashboard Bot Config → Sessions → Group reply conditions, or regularGroupMentionMode in bots.json
Single group	Only the current group	Send /mention-mode in the group (written to chatMentionModes in bots.json)

Change it with a command in the group

Send in a regular group (in a multi-bot group, @ the specific bot):

@bot /mention-mode status     # show the mode this group uses
@bot /mention-mode always
@bot /mention-mode topic
@bot /mention-mode never
@bot /mention-mode ambient

Viewing (status or no argument): talk access is enough.

Changing: requires operate rights (owner / allowedUsers).

Changes apply immediately, affect only this group, and leave the bot default alone.

Setting a group to the same value as the bot default means "follow the default again": if the bot default changes later, this group changes too. (Exception: bots with signedChatDefaults on keep the setting as written; see "Trusted group-creation service" at the end.)

Which groups support it

Only regular groups:

DMs: never need an @.

Topic groups: already topic-shaped; the command replies "no need to set it here".

Session groups created by /group: managed by the bot itself; changes are rejected.

Mode is always — why does it still answer without an @?

"Must be @-mentioned" is the default rule, but a set of parallel exceptions exists; matching any one makes the bot answer. When the bot "won't listen", it is almost always one of these:

#	Case	Notes
1	A reply continuing this bot's topic	The topic is already known to be addressed to this bot (e.g. a thread reply folded back into the group session), so it goes through
2	Substitute trigger	The bot has substitute mode on and the message @-mentions a person being covered (see "Substitute mode" below)
3	Message listener match	A listening rule configured under Dashboard Message Listener matched. This ignores the mention policy and the regular talk check; listeners have their own sender filters
4	Mode is never	The bot default or this group is set to no @ anywhere
5	Mode is ambient and the message doesn't @ anyone else	
6	Mode is topic and the message is inside a topic this bot handles	
7	No-@ slash commands	Commands listed in Dashboard Bot Config → Sessions → Slash commands without @ (e.g. /solve) fire when sent bare in a regular group. Only the listed commands are opened up, not the whole group
8	Built-in no-@ commands	/dash and /dashboard link never need an @, in any group
9	Group manager	This bot is the group's manager (default responder) and takes top-level non-@ messages. Turn on Group manager (default responder) under Bot Config → Sessions first. See the "Group manager" section in Slash Commands
10	1-person-1-bot group	Only you and this bot are in the group; no @ needed by default. You can turn this off — see the next section

A few details:

Except for message listeners (case 3), every case requires the sender to have talk access.

Cases 7, 8 and 9 also yield to explicit naming: if the message starts by @-mentioning someone else, the bot doesn't take it. But in /solve @someone, the @ after the command is an argument, so the command still fires.

In multi-bot groups where bots shouldn't talk over each other, prefer ambient: whoever is named answers.

Tip: sent a message and forgot the @? Use Lark's Edit to add an @ to this bot — that triggers it too.

Substitute mode: answer when someone else is @-mentioned

Substitute mode makes the bot a stand-in for certain people: when someone in a group @-mentions one of them (without @-mentioning the bot), the bot answers on their behalf. It suits people who get @-mentioned with questions all the time, such as the on-call engineer or a project owner.

Turn it on

In Dashboard Bot Config → Sessions → Substitute mode, turn on Enable substitute trigger and add substitute targets. Changes take effect as soon as you save.

You can enter an email directly. On save it is resolved to this app's Open ID; entries that fail to resolve are marked red and not saved.

You can also enter an Open ID, User ID, or Union ID. An Open ID must belong to this bot's app; Open IDs from other apps, and people outside the app's contact visibility scope, are rejected.

Turning it on needs at least one matchable target, otherwise saving fails.

The sender still needs talk access; substitute mode does not loosen permissions. To let everyone in a group ask by @-mentioning a target, combine it with On-Call Mode.

Which messages trigger it

Only text and rich-text messages where the sender typed the @ themselves. @-mentions carried in by a forwarded card or a merged forward don't count.

If the message @-mentions a target but its body starts with / (a slash command), it doesn't trigger; the @ in the command is treated as an argument and the message keeps its normal routing.

When trigger keywords are configured, the body must also contain one of them, otherwise the bot doesn't answer and the message is dropped outright — it won't fall through to any other path (existing session, no-@ modes, solo groups) (see keywords below).

Regular groups: the substitute turn goes into the group's group-scope session, and the reply is anchored to the trigger message.

Topic groups: the substitute turn goes into that topic's own session (a new one is started if none exists), and the reply stays in the topic.

Settings

Each Dashboard field maps to substituteMode in this bot's bots.json entry:

{
  "substituteMode": {
    "enabled": true,
    "targets": [
      { "openId": "ou_example", "name": "On-call engineer" }
    ],
    "keywords": ["incident", "oncall"],
    "disclosure": "prefix",
    "replyMode": "thread",
    "chats": [],
    "excludedChats": ["oc_example"],
    "topicGroups": true,
    "topicActiveSessionTrigger": true,
    "disableControlCard": false
  }
}

Field	Dashboard name	Meaning
enabled	Enable substitute trigger	Master switch. Turning it off keeps the targets and other settings, so you don't re-enter them next time
targets	Substitute targets	The people or bots being covered. Each entry has one of openId / userId / unionId; a bot can also be given by appId alone (see below). name is an optional display name shown to the AI
keywords	Trigger keywords (optional)	Array of strings. Empty or omitted means "trigger on @-mentioning a target alone". When set, a message must both @-mention a target and contain any of these keywords (case-insensitive substring match) in the body the sender typed in this message — mention labels, quoted/forwarded or history content are excluded, and a body that can't be parsed counts as no match. On a keyword miss the whole message is dropped and the bot stays silent; it never falls through to an existing session, no-@ mode or solo-group fallback (except when the bot itself is @-mentioned directly, or the body starts with / as a slash command). In the Dashboard, separate keywords with newlines, commas or semicolons
disclosure	Disclosure	prefix (default): ask the AI to say who it is answering for; none: no extra disclosure requirement
replyMode	Reply style	Regular groups only. thread (default): reply in a thread under the trigger message; quote: quote the trigger message without a new thread
chats	Allowed chats	Allow-list. Empty means every group; when filled, it triggers only in these groups
excludedChats	Blocked chats	Never triggers in these groups, and /substitute on in the group can't turn it back on. A group in both lists is blocked
topicGroups	Topic groups	On by default. Set to false to trigger only in regular groups
topicActiveSessionTrigger	Trigger in topics with an active session	On by default. Set to false and, in a topic where this bot already has a session, @-mentioning a target counts as a hand-off: the bot stays quiet
disableControlCard	Send owner control card	When a substitute session starts in a regular group, the owner / allowedUsers get a DM control card (open terminal, restart, close) by default. Set to true to skip it. Topic groups keep their normal streaming card, with no extra DM

A few notes:

When editing bots.json by hand, an email-only target matches no one: Lark @-mentions don't carry email. The email is only kept as a label; if substitute mode is enabled but no target has an openId / userId / unionId / appId, the whole substituteMode block is ignored on load. To add people by email, save them in the Dashboard so they are resolved to Open IDs.

Run botmux restart after editing by hand.

In a blocked group, a message that @-mentions a target is ignored outright and doesn't fall through to other no-@ rules. Direct @-mentions of the bot are still answered.

Bot substitute targets by App ID

To have the bot answer for another bot, choose App ID as the target type and enter cli_...; in bots.json write { "appId": "cli_example" }. No Open ID or chat ID is needed, and display names are never used for matching.

@-mentions in both text and rich-text messages count, whether a person or a bot with talk access sent them.

The allow list, block list, per-group /substitute off, trigger keywords and active-topic rules work exactly as for Open ID targets, and a message they hold back doesn't fall through to other paths either. Messages from bots go through the same rules; when one is held back it also doesn't start a session through new-topic auto-start.

Lark events only carry the receiver-scoped Open ID, so the bot reads the message again through the Get Message API to learn the App ID. If that read fails, returns a different version of the message, or the identities don't line up, the message isn't treated as an App ID substitute trigger.

When a substitute message from a bot waits in the session queue, the sender's access and the substitute settings are checked again right before it runs. If the sender is revoked or blocked, or substitute mode is turned off or changed meanwhile, the message is dropped.

Saving only checks the format (uppercase is converted to lowercase). It doesn't check that the app exists or is in the group, and doesn't request extra scopes to look up names. A malformed appId in a hand-edited bots.json is logged as a warning and that target is ignored.

Per-group toggle

Substitute mode is on by default in every group it applies to. To switch it off for one group, @ the bot in that group:

@bot /substitute status     # check whether it's on in this group
@bot /substitute off        # turn it off in this group
@bot /substitute on         # turn it back on in this group

Anyone can check status; switching needs operate access (owner / allowedUsers).

Works in regular and topic groups, not in DMs.

If the group is blocked, or it is a topic group while topicGroups is off, the command tells you it can't be used here instead of pretending it was turned on.

Turn off "no @ in 1-person-1-bot groups"

A group with one human and one bot needs no @ by default. To make these groups follow the mention policy, configure the bot's bots.json entry:

{
  "regularGroupMentionMode": "always",
  "soloGroupMentionBypass": false,
  "chatSoloGroupMentionBypass": {
    "oc_example": true
  }
}

Field	Meaning
soloGroupMentionBypass	Bot-level switch. Omitted or true: keep the no-@ exception; false: turn it off
chatSoloGroupMentionBypass	Per-group overrides. Explicit true / false beats the bot-level switch; remove a group's entry to inherit again

In the example, only oc_example keeps the exception; all other groups have it off. To turn it off for just one group, keep the bot default and set that group to false in the map.

Run botmux restart after editing by hand.

Once it's off:

The effective mention policy (per-group first) decides: always needs @; topic still allows non-@ follow-ups in topics the bot handles; never / ambient behave as usual.

Under always / topic, non-@ top-level text or images no longer start a session just because the group is small.

The switch applies to regular and topic groups, not DMs; permission checks and "yield when someone else is named" still apply.

This switch only removes the implicit "small group" exception. Message listeners, no-@ commands, substitutes, and auto-start on group join / new topic are separate settings. For strict @-only behavior: set the switch to false, set the group's mention policy to always, and check that the group has no other triggers enabled.

Also, "1 person, 1 bot" is judged by group membership. When a message @-mentions another member, the bot re-checks membership, so an old bot won't grab the turn right after a new bot joins. If the mentioned person isn't in the group (Lark allows mentioning non-members) and the re-check still shows one human and one bot, the exception still applies.

Advanced: trusted group-creation service

If your deployment uses a trusted group-creation service and signedChatDefaults is enabled in bots.json, groups created by that service default to ambient. The order then is: the group's /mention-mode setting → the service-declared ambient → the bot default. This only affects whether an @ is needed; it never loosens permissions.

Related: whether a reply lands in a new topic or the current session is controlled by /reply-mode; see Slash Commands.

title: Model Proxy (Experimental)
content:
⚠️ Experimental: endpoints, fields and limits may change. It does not affect regular Feishu bots.

botmux model-proxy serve starts an authenticated, OpenAI Chat Completions–compatible endpoint on 127.0.0.1. Tools that only speak the OpenAI protocol (scripts built on the OpenAI SDK, code-review tools, and so on) can point their baseURL here and call models through a CLI's own login (Codex, Claude Code, …) — no separate API key needed.

Your tool (OpenAI SDK)
   │  HTTP + Bearer token, 127.0.0.1 only
   ▼
botmux model-proxy (this page)
   │  local signed IPC
   ▼
Dedicated core-only instance (apiOnly bot with its own native login)
   │
   ▼
Native CLI model call (all tools disabled, inference only)

When to use it

I want to…	Use this?
Let an existing OpenAI-protocol tool reuse a CLI's model login	✅ That's what it's for
My tool manages context and tool calls itself and only needs a "model endpoint"	✅ Tool calls come back as proposals; your tool executes them
Have AI work and edit code in Feishu	❌ Use a regular bot, see Quick Start
Drive a full CLI session over HTTP (read/write files, run commands)	❌ See Core-only (apiOnly) API control
Streaming, embeddings, images, audio, direct browser access	❌ Not supported yet

Key points up front:

Loopback only (127.0.0.1). The config only accepts this address, so it is not reachable from the network.

The CLI never touches your files: native CLI tools are disabled on every call; it only does inference. Returned tool_calls are proposals — execution stays with your tool.

No borrowed logins: the proxy only uses the login in the dedicated bot directory you specify. It never picks up chat bots', the global, or other bots' credentials.

Quick start

Step 1: Start a dedicated core-only instance

The proxy doesn't call models itself. It forwards requests to a separate core-only instance (a botmux that doesn't connect to Feishu and only serves local HTTP, see Core-only). That instance must:

Be its own process with its own data directory and port. Do not reuse — or restart for this — a running Feishu bot daemon.

Have a bot ID of the form local_<name>, using only letters, digits, _ and - in the name (the proxy config rejects .).

Use one of the supported CLIs below, with a native login completed in that bot's dedicated directory.

export STATE_DIR="$HOME/model-proxy-demo"     # pick a fresh directory
export BOTMUX_CORE_CLI=codex                  # or claude-code / pi / opencode
export BOTMUX_API_ONLY_BOT=local_reasoner
export BOTMUX_CORE_CODEX_AUTH_SYNC=isolated   # Codex only
export BOTMUX_CORE_STATE_DIR="$STATE_DIR/data"
export BOTMUX_API_PORT=8930                   # pick a free port
botmux serve --api-only

This command runs in the foreground. Use another terminal for the next steps, and export STATE_DIR=... again there (same directory as above).

Login files live under $STATE_DIR/bots/<bot ID>/<subdir>:

CLI	Subdir	Login files needed
codex / codex-app	codex	auth.json, plus a models_cache.json that contains the target model; BOTMUX_CORE_CODEX_AUTH_SYNC=isolated is required
claude-code	claude	.credentials.json (a login that only lives in the system keychain won't work)
pi	pi	auth.json (API key or OAuth; executable helpers not supported)
opencode	opencode	auth.json (API / OAuth records only)

For Codex, for example, log that directory in with CODEX_HOME="$STATE_DIR/bots/local_reasoner/codex" codex login.

Keep this instance "plain": no sandbox, no --backend, no extra env vars, startup commands or wrapper. With any of these, the proxy refuses to start with inference_profile_unsupported.

Step 2: Write the proxy config file

Save the following to a file, e.g. $STATE_DIR/model-proxy.json:

{
  "port": 8788,
  "models": {
    "review-model": {
      "bot": "local_reasoner",
      "model": "<native-model-id>",
      "deadlineMs": 120000
    }
  },
  "clients": [
    { "id": "review-client", "tokenEnv": "BOTMUX_MODEL_PROXY_TOKEN", "models": ["review-model"] }
  ]
}

Lock it down so only you can read and write it, otherwise the proxy won't start:

export PROXY_CONFIG="$STATE_DIR/model-proxy.json"
chmod 600 "$PROXY_CONFIG"

It must be a regular file owned by the current user with mode exactly 0600.

Its directory (and the directories above it) must not be writable by other users.

Step 3: Create a token and start the proxy

# At least 32 characters, no whitespace; hand it to the tool over a secure channel
export BOTMUX_MODEL_PROXY_TOKEN="$(openssl rand -hex 32)"
# Point at the data directory of the Step 1 instance so the proxy can find it
export SESSION_DATA_DIR="$STATE_DIR/data"
botmux model-proxy serve --config "$PROXY_CONFIG"

On success it prints one line of JSON:

{"listening":"http://127.0.0.1:8788/v1","protocol":"chat-completions-v1"}

The proxy runs in the foreground. Ctrl+C (SIGINT) or SIGTERM stops it and cancels calls still in flight.

Step 4: Connect your tool

const client = new OpenAI({
  baseURL: 'http://127.0.0.1:8788/v1',
  apiKey: process.env.BOTMUX_MODEL_PROXY_TOKEN,
  maxRetries: 0, // retries are your call; send an Idempotency-Key if you need dedup
});

const result = await client.chat.completions.create({
  model: 'review-model', // the alias from the config, not the native model name
  messages: [{ role: 'user', content: 'Explain binary search in one sentence.' }],
});
console.log(result.choices[0].message.content);

To check connectivity first, list the models this token can use:

curl -s http://127.0.0.1:8788/v1/models \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $BOTMUX_MODEL_PROXY_TOKEN"

Config file reference

Top-level fields

Field	Required	Description
host	No	Must be 127.0.0.1 (the default)
port	No	Listening port, default 8788; 0 lets the OS pick one
models	Yes	Model alias table, at least one entry
clients	Yes	Clients allowed to connect, 1–100

Unknown fields in the config are rejected, not ignored.

models: model aliases

Clients only see the alias (e.g. review-model), never which bot or native model is behind it.

Field	Required	Description
bot	Yes	Bot ID of the Step 1 dedicated instance, e.g. local_reasoner
model	Yes	Native model name, as understood by the CLI
reasoningEffort	No	Reasoning effort: none / minimal / low / medium / high / xhigh / max / ultra; ultimately bounded by what the CLI supports
deadlineMs	No	Per-call time limit, 100–300000 ms, default 120000; returns 504 on timeout

clients: clients and tokens

Field	Description
id	Client name (letters, digits, _, -), must be unique
tokenEnv	Name of the env var holding the token (starts with an uppercase letter, e.g. BOTMUX_MODEL_PROXY_TOKEN). The token itself never goes in the config file
models	Aliases this client may use; all must exist in models

Tokens must be at least 32 characters with no whitespace; different clients can't share a token.

The token is unrelated to the CLI's subscription credentials — it only decides which aliases are allowed.

Changing a token requires restarting the proxy.

Supported endpoints and fields

There are only two endpoints, both requiring Authorization: Bearer <token>:

GET /v1/models: lists the aliases this token may use.

POST /v1/chat/completions: non-streaming chat completion; Content-Type must be application/json.

Field	Support
model	Required; an alias that is in this client's allow list
messages	Five roles: system / developer / user / assistant / tool; content is a string or an array of text parts only; up to 2000 messages
tools	function type only, up to 128; parameter schema must be an object
tool_choice	auto / none / required / a specific function
parallel_tool_calls	When false, at most one call proposal is returned
response_format	text, json_object, json_schema
stream / n	Omit them, or use stream: false, n: 1
max_completion_tokens	Omitted or null means no limit specified; an integer 1–128000 is only supported by Claude Code — other CLIs return 400 max_completion_tokens_unsupported
Anything else	Always 400 unsupported_or_invalid_parameter, including temperature, top_p, max_tokens, seed, stop, logprobs, etc. — never silently ignored

Supported JSON Schema keywords for tool parameters and json_schema: type, properties, required, boolean additionalProperties, items, enum, description, title, numeric bounds, string length, array length. $ref, combinators like anyOf/oneOf, regex patterns and the like are not supported and are rejected.

Multi-turn tool calls

Same as with OpenAI: the model returns tool_calls → your tool executes them → send the results back as tool messages (with tool_call_id) in the next request. The proxy checks that history is complete:

tool_call_ids must be unique, and every call needs a matching result.

No other message may be inserted before all results are in.

The model's answer is validated too: calling an unknown function, arguments that don't match the schema, violating tool_choice, or invalid JSON when JSON was requested all return 502 instead of handing you a bad result as success.

What comes back

On success finish_reason is stop or tool_calls. length is never returned.

Tool call IDs are generated deterministically, so replaying an idempotent request keeps the same IDs.

The standard usage field is always null. Real usage is in botmux.native_invocation_usage, which totals the whole CLI invocation (possibly including internal retries) and can't be treated as a single API bill. Some tools display null as 0 — that doesn't mean nothing was consumed.

Idempotency and timeouts

With an Idempotency-Key header (alphanumerics and _.:-, up to 128 chars), the same key + same request from the same client and alias replays the stored result without calling the CLI again; same key with a different request returns 409.

Two requests without a key are two independent calls.

A client disconnect cancels the call; within one proxy process, if several connections wait on the same result, one disconnecting doesn't affect the others.

Run one proxy process per inference bot.

Common errors

Errors always look like {"error":{"message":"<code>","type":"...","param":...,"code":"<code>"}} and never include CLI error output, credentials or local paths.

Status	Common causes
400	Unsupported or malformed field (check which field param points to), incomplete tool history
401	Wrong token or missing Authorization
403	Alias not allowed for this token; or the request carries an Origin header (direct browser access isn't supported)
404	Unsupported endpoint
409	Idempotency key conflict, or the call was cancelled
413	Request body over 1 MB, or the assembled prompt is too long
415	Content-Type isn't application/json, or a content encoding was used
429	Inference instance is at capacity
502	Inference failed or the model output failed validation, e.g. native_auth_missing (dedicated directory not logged in), native_model_not_found (wrong model name)
503	Dedicated instance not found (inference_profile_offline), instance config doesn't qualify (inference_profile_unsupported), transport failure
504	deadlineMs exceeded

FAQ

Startup fails with model_proxy_config_missing or a permission error?
Check that the --config path exists, the file is chmod 600, and its directory isn't writable by other users.

Startup fails with model_proxy_token_requires_32_nonwhitespace_characters?
The env var named by tokenEnv isn't set, or the token is too short or contains whitespace.

Getting inference_profile_offline?
The proxy can't find the dedicated instance. Make sure it's running and that SESSION_DATA_DIR points at its data directory ($STATE_DIR/data from Step 1) when you start the proxy.

Is it exactly the same as calling the model API directly?
Not exactly. Conversation roles and tool definitions are serialized into text for the CLI, then the response is rebuilt from structured output. Role order and tool associations are preserved, but this isn't native verbatim passthrough, and the CLI's internal prompts and retries also affect results.

Can the output limit be used as a cost cap?
No. max_completion_tokens only applies to Claude's generation request; the CLI's wrapping and retries also consume tokens.

Related

Core-only (apiOnly) API control: starting the dedicated instance, data directory and security boundaries

CLI commands

Supported CLIs

Step 2: Write the proxy config file
Step 3: Create a token and start the proxy
