title: Plugin Development and Publishing
content:
A Botmux plugin is one npm package. Once installed, it can give the Agent Skills and MCP tools, add subcommands to the botmux CLI, add a page to the Dashboard, run a long-lived background service, and register Feishu /slash commands and card buttons.

Start with what you want to do:

I want to…	Go to
Install an existing plugin and turn it on for a Bot	Install and manage plugins
Write a plugin from scratch	Five-minute start → Building each contribution
Publish to npm and list it in the Plugin Market	Publish to npm → Register in the Plugin Market

Installing a third-party plugin means trusting its author: plugin code runs as the system user that runs Botmux. Confirmed Dashboard installs skip npm lifecycle scripts; ordinary CLI installs may still run them. Only install packages you trust. A catalog listing is not a security endorsement.

What a plugin can provide

A plugin delivers its capabilities through fixed directories. Botmux scans them at install time, so nothing else needs registering. Every entry lives in the build output dist/:

Capability	Purpose	Entry after install (relative to dist/)
Skill	Instructions for the Agent	skills/<name>/SKILL.md
MCP	Tools for the Agent (at most one server per plugin)	mcp/index.json
CLI commands	Ops entry points shaped like botmux <command>	cli/index.js + cli/commands.json
Dashboard page	A plugin page inside the Dashboard	dashboard/index.js
Dashboard settings	Server-side adapter the page uses to read/write config (optional)	server/settings.js
Host Service	A long-running background process, e.g. a local HTTP service	service/index.js
Feishu slash commands	/xxx in a chat goes straight to the plugin	commands/index.json (needs a Host Service)
Card button callbacks	Button clicks on the plugin's cards go to the plugin	card-actions/index.json (needs a Host Service)

There is no general daemon/worker hook. Put long-running logic in a Host Service, Agent capabilities in MCP or a Skill, and human-facing ops entry points in CLI commands.

Five-minute start

Plugin development needs Node.js 22+ with npm on PATH: the generator uses npm to scaffold, install dependencies, and run tests. (That is only a requirement for developing plugins. Botmux itself is a self-contained binary and does not need Node; see Quick Start.)

# 1. Install botmux (either way)
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/deepcoldy/botmux/master/install.sh | sh
# npm install -g botmux@latest

# 2. Generate a plugin project
botmux plugin init my-plugin
cd botmux-plugin-my-plugin

# 3. Install in development mode and enable it
botmux plugin install . --link
botmux plugin enable my-plugin

# 4. Try the sample command
botmux my-plugin:hello

plugin init creates the project from the official template and runs npm install and npm test for you (git init is best-effort; failing it is fine). Defaults:

Item	Default
Directory	botmux-plugin-my-plugin
npm package name	@botmux-ai/plugin-my-plugin
Plugin ID	my-plugin
CLI command prefix	my-plugin:
Samples	One for each basic contribution type

@botmux-ai is the official npm organization. If you can't publish to that scope, change name in package.json to a package you control, such as @your-org/plugin-my-plugin. The Plugin ID can stay my-plugin, but third-party packages must be installed by their full package name.

Install and manage plugins

Install

# Third-party package: use the full name, ideally pinned to an exact version
botmux plugin install @your-org/plugin-my-plugin@1.2.3

# Official short ID: expands to @botmux-ai/plugin-my-plugin
botmux plugin install my-plugin

# A local directory or a packed tarball
botmux plugin install ./path/to/plugin
botmux plugin install "file:/absolute/path/plugin-package.tgz"

Installing does three things: download, validate the manifest, and scan the contribution entries, then store dist/ under ~/.botmux/plugins/<id>/. Installing does not run plugin code and does not start the Service.

Enable: choose which Bots it applies to

After installing, enable the plugin so it shows up in sessions:

# Machine default: applies to every Bot (including Bots added later)
botmux plugin enable my-plugin

# One Bot only; all = write an entry for each currently configured Bot
botmux plugin enable my-plugin --bot <name|index|all>

# Turn it off
botmux plugin disable my-plugin
botmux plugin disable my-plugin --bot <name|index|all>

Without --bot you get the machine-default scope (stored as plugins in ~/.botmux/config.json). There is no --global.

Per-Bot enablement is stored in that Bot's plugins field in bots.json and adds to the machine default.

If a plugin is already enabled as machine default, turn the machine default off before configuring it per Bot.

After enabling, disabling, or updating, start a new session. A running CLI does not hot-load new Skills/MCP. Feishu slash commands are the exception: they take effect on the next message.

botmux plugin list shows installed plugins and whether each is enabled as machine default.

Manage from the Dashboard

The 插件 (Plugins) page has Installed and Discover views using the Dashboard's light and dark themes.

Installed supports search and source filtering. Cards show the name, description, audience, enablement and management action.

Management retains machine-default and per-Bot enablement, settings and sidebar pinning. Package details, contribution lists and service controls are under collapsed Advanced settings.

Discover reads the plugin catalog, with search, details and installation. Network failures show cached results or an explicit unavailable state.

Installation confirmation displays the package name, exact npm version and SHA-512 integrity. It is bound to the management identity, expires after five minutes and must be repeated if the registry state or management credentials change. Installation does not automatically enable a plugin.

Uninstall requires disabling all scopes and stopping the service before confirming the package and version. The installer rechecks the confirmation before committing changes.

Install and uninstall require the local management identity and CSRF validation. Discovery needs network access; installation also needs npm and tar on PATH. Packages must ship a prebuilt dist/, rather than generating runtime files in install scripts.

Card descriptions come from npm package.json's description. Optional botmux.audience describes the intended audience or prerequisites. These are display fields, not authorization controls.

A plugin's own page lives at #/plugins/<plugin-id>. For more on the Dashboard, see Dashboard.

Manage the Host Service

botmux plugin service status
botmux plugin service start my-plugin      # or --all
botmux plugin service stop my-plugin
botmux plugin service restart my-plugin

A Service has one of two modes (declared in the manifest):

Mode	Behavior
manual (default)	Starts only when you run plugin service start
auto	botmux start / botmux restart make sure it is running

botmux stop keeps plugin Services running by default; botmux stop --with-plugin stops auto Services too.

botmux restart does not stop auto Services first by default; botmux restart --with-plugin stops them and starts them again.

Services are managed by Botmux's built-in supervisor; you don't need PM2. Logs are in ~/.botmux/plugin-supervisor/logs/<plugin-id>-out.log and -err.log.

Update and uninstall

To update, install the new version again. If the plugin has a Service, stop it first. Botmux does not stop a Service for you during install, update, or uninstall; a running Service makes the command fail:

botmux plugin service stop my-plugin
botmux plugin install @your-org/plugin-my-plugin@1.2.4
botmux plugin enable my-plugin
botmux plugin service start my-plugin

Uninstall:

botmux plugin service stop my-plugin
botmux plugin uninstall my-plugin

Uninstalling removes the plugin's enablement from every scope and deletes the whole ~/.botmux/plugins/<id>/ directory (including plugin config), so back it up first if you need it. It is refused while other enabled plugins depend on it. The --force flag shown in help currently cannot bypass dependency or Service protections.

Tune a plugin's MCP per Bot

To give one Bot's plugin MCP different environment variables or its own timeout, add pluginRuntime to that Bot in bots.json:

{
  "plugins": ["reporting"],
  "pluginRuntime": {
    "reporting": {
      "env": { "PROFILE": "production" },
      "toolTimeoutMs": 120000
    }
  }
}

Field	Meaning
env	Injected only into this plugin's local stdio MCP process for this Bot; never into the model CLI's environment
toolTimeoutMs	Total timeout per tool call for this plugin (milliseconds, positive integer); defaults to the MCP SDK default

The machine-wide ceiling is mcpGatewayMaxToolTimeoutMs in ~/.botmux/config.json, default 600000 (10 minutes). toolTimeoutMs can't exceed this ceiling; if it does, preparing plugins for a new session fails with an error. Changes apply on the next CLI cold start or new session.

package.json and the manifest

The plugin's root package.json is both the npm package description and the plugin manifest (the botmux field). Full example:

{
  "name": "@your-org/plugin-my-plugin",
  "version": "0.1.0",
  "description": "Botmux plugin: My Plugin.",
  "type": "module",
  "keywords": ["botmux-plugin"],
  "scripts": {
    "build": "node ./scripts/build.mjs",
    "validate": "node ./scripts/validate.mjs",
    "test": "npm run build && npm run validate",
    "prepublishOnly": "npm test"
  },
  "botmux": {
    "schemaVersion": 1,
    "id": "my-plugin",
    "displayName": "My Plugin",
    "dependencies": {
      "plugins": ["another-plugin"]
    },
    "service": {
      "mode": "manual"
    }
  },
  "files": ["dist/"],
  "publishConfig": {
    "registry": "https://registry.npmjs.org/",
    "access": "public"
  },
  "license": "MIT"
}

Install-time checks:

version is valid SemVer;

keywords contains botmux-plugin;

botmux.id matches ^[a-z][a-z0-9._-]{0,63}$;

the package contains a dist/ directory;

service.mode is manual or auto (defaults to manual);

every contribution entry exists and is well-formed.

botmux.dependencies.plugins lists Plugin IDs only; version ranges are not supported. To enable a plugin, its dependencies must be installed and enabled in the same scope. A plugin that other enabled plugins depend on cannot be disabled or uninstalled.

Keep files limited to dist/ and check npm pack --dry-run before publishing. npm still includes package.json, README, and LICENSE automatically, so make sure those contain nothing sensitive either.

Building each contribution

CLI commands

src/cli/index.js default-exports a "command name → handler" object. The official template's build emits both dist/cli/index.js and the command index dist/cli/commands.json:

export default {
  "my-plugin:hello": {
    description: "Print a hello response.",
    run(ctx) {
      return JSON.stringify({
        pluginId: ctx.pluginId,
        version: ctx.version,
        args: ctx.args,
      });
    },
  },
};

Users call it directly as botmux my-plugin:hello [args...].

Command names must match ^[a-z][a-z0-9._:-]{0,63}$. Botmux adds no namespace, and two enabled plugins with the same command name fail with a conflict, so always prefix with <plugin-id>:.

If run returns a string it is printed; a number becomes the exit code.

From a host terminal, only machine-default plugins are searched; inside an Agent session, the plugins enabled for that session are searched.

ctx gives you:

pluginId, pluginDir, packageName, version, manifest, args;

api.logger, api.resolve(relativePath);

api.config.get/set/replace: read and write the plugin's private config at ~/.botmux/plugins/<id>/config.json;

api.settingsPath.

Skill

Write it at skills/<skill-name>/SKILL.md during development; after the build it must be at dist/skills/<skill-name>/SKILL.md.

After enabling or updating, a running Agent does not hot-load the new Skill. Start a new session and Botmux regenerates the plugin and Skill snapshot for that CLI process.

MCP

Each plugin can provide at most one MCP server, declared in dist/mcp/index.json. Two transports are supported.

Local process (stdio):

{
  "transport": "stdio",
  "command": ["node", "./mcp/server.js"],
  "env": {}
}

Remote HTTP (Streamable HTTP):

{
  "transport": "streamable-http",
  "url": "https://example.com/mcp",
  "headers": {}
}

Things to know:

only stdio and streamable-http are supported;

the MCP name is the Plugin ID automatically, so don't add name;

./... paths are relative to the installed dist/;

${VAR} string templates are not supported; to vary settings per Bot, use pluginRuntime above;

bundle a local MCP's runtime dependencies into dist/ instead of relying on the development node_modules;

never put real tokens, cookies, or secrets in the package; read them at runtime from a controlled environment or the plugin's private config.

Botmux aggregates the MCP servers of all plugins enabled for the current session through one MCP Gateway. When tools from different plugins share a name, the Gateway adds a prefix to tell them apart. The plugin set and credential snapshot are fixed per CLI process, so start a new session after changing enablement or config.

Trusted caller identity

When a turn is triggered by a real Feishu user, the Gateway attaches a caller identity to forwarded tools/call requests. It is stamped by the host and cannot be forged by the model, so plugins can enforce per-user permissions or audit.

Where to read it:

_meta.botmuxTrustedCaller on the MCP request (both stdio and streamable-http). Common fields:
Field	Meaning
requestUserOpenId / requestUserUnionId	The user who triggered this turn
requestLarkAppId	The current Bot's Feishu app ID
senderType	user or bot: whether a human or another Bot opened this turn; absent when it can't be determined
source / taskId	No source = an ordinary Feishu message; schedule_creator = a scheduled task running as its creator/claimer (taskId is the task ID); failed_turn_recovery = an automatic retry of a failed request, not a new human action
turnId / dispatchAttempt	This turn's ID and delivery attempt, useful for idempotency

streamable-http also gets request headers: x-botmux-trusted-open-id, x-botmux-trusted-union-id, x-botmux-trusted-app-id, plus x-botmux-turn-id and x-botmux-dispatch-attempt. The headers do not carry source, taskId, or senderType; read _meta when you need them.

How to use it safely:

Trust only keys in the botmux namespace. Before forwarding, the Gateway unconditionally strips any _meta key starting with botmux that the model supplied, as well as inbound x-botmux-trusted-* headers, so the model cannot impersonate someone else.

Don't treat bare keys (such as an un-namespaced requestUserUnionId or a custom trustedCaller) as identity. They are not stripped and the model can fill them freely.

Not every turn has a user identity: turns without a sender ID carry no requestUserOpenId / requestUserUnionId (botmuxTrustedCaller may hold only turnId). Fail closed when those user fields are missing (refuse identity-gated operations) and never fall back to values the model reports.

To confirm "a human just asked for this", check senderType === "user" and that source is absent.

The host injects the identity per turn. Don't show it to users, and don't log it together with transport tokens.

Keep sensitive results away from the model

Some tool results (business data, report files) shouldn't go to the model. A local stdio MCP can declare a result in the tool response's _meta.botmuxHostDelivery, and Botmux delivers it straight to the requester:

{
  "schemaVersion": 1,
  "deliveryId": "report-20261105-0001",
  "markdown": "## Monthly report\n…",
  "files": [{ "path": "report.xlsx" }]
}

A "结果已生成" (result ready) card appears in the chat. Its "查看或下载" (view or download) button opens a host-controlled page that only the requester of this turn can see, and the link expires;

the model only gets a receipt (delivered, deliveryId, fileCount), never the raw result;

attachments must live under ~/.botmux/plugins/<id>/outbound/ and are deleted after successful delivery; up to 8 files, each ≤ 8 MiB, ≤ 16 MiB in total;

only local stdio MCP servers can use it, and the turn must carry a trusted human identity; otherwise the tool call fails.

botmuxTrustedCaller.hostCapabilities containing result_delivery_v1 means the current host supports it.

Dashboard page

src/dashboard/index.js default-exports a component:

export default function PluginDashboard({ pluginId, api }) {
  return `Dashboard loaded for ${pluginId}`;
}

The route is fixed at #/plugins/<plugin-id>. api provides:

Method	Purpose
react	The host's React instance; reuse it instead of bundling another copy
getServiceStatus()	Read this plugin's Service status
startService() / stopService() / restartService()	Control this plugin's Service
getSettings() / saveSettings(value)	Read/write config through the settings adapter
listBots()	List manageable Bots

Settings adapter: to use getSettings / saveSettings, ship dist/server/settings.js exporting both functions:

export function getSettings(api: { config: PluginConfigApi }): unknown | Promise<unknown>;
export function saveSettings(api: { config: PluginConfigApi }, value: unknown): unknown | Promise<unknown>;

The injected api has only config: get(key?), set(key, value), replace(object), and path. There is no logger, resolve, or settingsPath.

Return only fields that are safe to show in a browser; don't echo raw config.json or secrets.

Return values must be JSON-serializable; returning null/undefined gives the browser { "ok": true }.

Errors: invalid request JSON → 400; plugin missing or no adapter → 404; unsupported method → 405; plugin updated or replaced while the save was waiting → 409 plugin_settings_stale (reload and retry); adapter throws, bad exports, or unserializable result → 500 with the single code plugin_settings_failed, never the raw exception.

The install scan does not run adapter code; exports are checked at request time.

Dashboard code runs within the permissions of the system user that installed Botmux. Don't render sensitive config into the page or browser logs.

Host Service

A Service needs both of these:

botmux.service.mode in package.json;

dist/service/index.js.

Example:

export default {
  mode: "manual",
  port: 9360,
  pm2: {
    script: "./service/server.js",
    env: {
      PORT: "9360",
    },
    autorestart: true,
  },
  urls({ host, port }) {
    return {
      openUrl: `http://${host}:${port}/`,
      healthUrl: `http://${host}:${port}/health`,
    };
  },
};

The pm2 field name is kept only for compatibility with older plugins. Botmux's built-in supervisor interprets it; PM2 is not needed. Supported keys: script, args, cwd, env, autorestart, killTimeoutMs, watchDelayMs.

If the export sets mode, it must match the manifest.

The host passed to urls() is already URL-ready (IPv6 literals come bracketed).

The Service process receives BOTMUX_PLUGIN_ID, BOTMUX_PLUGIN_DIR, and BOTMUX_PLUGIN_HOME.

With the single-file Botmux binary, JS scripts run on its embedded Bun, so no separate Node install is needed.

While developing with --link, the Service restarts automatically when dist/ changes (only dist/botmux-build/ is watched if it exists).

Feishu slash commands

A plugin can register its own Feishu commands. For example, /work-bind status in a chat does not go to the CLI; it goes straight to the plugin's Host Service, and Botmux posts the plugin's text or card reply back to the chat.

Declare: ship dist/commands/index.json; the plugin must have a Host Service:

{
  "schemaVersion": 1,
  "endpoint": "/botmux/commands/v1",
  "commands": [
    { "name": "/work-bind", "description": "Bind or view this chat's work item" }
  ]
}

name must be a lowercase /xxx (letters, digits, : _ -), 1–16 per plugin, no duplicates;

it can't reuse a Botmux built-in or CLI passthrough command (such as /help, /close, /compact); that is rejected at install time;

description is optional, up to 120 characters, and is listed in the "🧩 Plugin commands" section at the end of /help;

endpoint is a relative path. Botmux builds http://127.0.0.1:<port><endpoint> itself, so the Service definition must set a fixed port.

What users see:

the sender must be allowed to talk to this Bot; no session is created, nothing goes to the CLI, and no quota is used;

in a regular group that requires @-mentioning the Bot (see Mention mode), plugin commands need the @ too;

if two enabled plugins declare the same command, it is disabled and the Bot replies that multiple plugins declared it;

if the Bot's customPassthroughCommands has the same name, passthrough wins;

if the plugin service is offline, times out (10 seconds), or returns something invalid, the Bot replies that the plugin command is unavailable; it never falls back to sending the message to the CLI;

enabling or disabling a plugin takes effect on the next message, no restart needed.

Request and response: Botmux sends a POST to the endpoint with Authorization: Bearer <token> (the token is in the Service's BOTMUX_PLUGIN_CARD_ACTION_TOKEN environment variable, shared with card callbacks). It is sent once, with no retry:

{
  "schemaVersion": 1,
  "eventId": "om_xxx",
  "larkAppId": "cli_xxx",
  "command": "/work-bind",
  "args": "status",
  "chat": { "chatId": "oc_xxx", "chatType": "group", "anchor": "om_xxx" },
  "sender": { "openId": "ou_xxx", "unionId": "on_xxx" },
  "privileges": { "canOperate": true, "canTalk": true },
  "locale": "zh"
}

eventId is the triggering message ID; use it for idempotency;

args already has the command name stripped;

privileges is computed by the host on the spot: canOperate means the sender can manage this Bot, canTalk means they can talk to it. Use only this for authorization; never infer identity or permissions from args.

The plugin replies:

{ "schemaVersion": 1, "reply": { "text": "Bound" } }

reply can be { "text": "…" } (up to 4000 characters), { "card": { … } }, or omitted (no reply). Button callbacks in the card may only use actions this plugin declared in card-actions.

Card button callbacks

Buttons on cards the plugin sends can be handled by the plugin when clicked.

Declare: ship dist/card-actions/index.json; it also needs a Host Service with a fixed port:

{
  "schemaVersion": 1,
  "endpoint": "/botmux/card-actions/v1",
  "actions": ["my-plugin.confirm"],
  "actionPrefixes": ["my-plugin."]
}

Provide at least one of actions (exact match) and actionPrefixes (prefix match); neither may overlap Botmux's own button actions;

a button's action name comes from its value.action, falling back to the button's name;

to send a card with plugin buttons from a session: botmux send --plugin-card-action my-plugin --card-file card.json (only together with --card-file / --card-json).

On click, Botmux POSTs the operator, card context, button value, and form values to the endpoint (same Bearer token), along with host-computed privileges. The plugin can reply:

{
  "schemaVersion": 1,
  "ack": {
    "toast": { "type": "success", "content": "Confirmed" },
    "card": { "schema": "2.0", "body": {} }
  }
}

toast is a short notice after the click (success / info / warning / error); card updates the card in place. Both are optional. The plugin must still check privileges on every click; permission at send time is not authorization at click time.

Local build and acceptance

During development:

npm install
npm test

botmux plugin install . --link
botmux plugin enable my-plugin
botmux my-plugin:hello

--link is for local directories only; it links the plugin runtime directory to your project's dist/. You still need to rebuild after editing source. After adding or removing contribution entries, run plugin install again so Botmux rescans.

Before publishing, verify again with a real tarball:

npm ci
npm test
npm pack --dry-run
npm pack

botmux plugin install "file:/absolute/path/plugin-package.tgz"
botmux plugin enable my-plugin
botmux plugin service start my-plugin   # skip if there is no Service
botmux plugin service status

The point is not "it runs inside the repo" but that the extracted dist/ works on its own, without the source tree or node_modules.

Publish to npm

Fill in repository metadata and confirm the package name is in an npm scope you control:

{
  "repository": {
    "type": "git",
    "url": "git+https://github.com/your-org/botmux-plugin-my-plugin.git"
  },
  "homepage": "https://github.com/your-org/botmux-plugin-my-plugin#readme",
  "bugs": {
    "url": "https://github.com/your-org/botmux-plugin-my-plugin/issues"
  }
}

Check that you are logged in (for an existing package you can also confirm owners with npm owner ls <package>; before the first publish the package doesn't exist yet and that returns 404, so skip it):

npm whoami --registry=https://registry.npmjs.org/

Publish the scoped public package:

npm publish --access public --registry=https://registry.npmjs.org/
Publishing must satisfy the account or package 2FA policy. For long-running CI, prefer npm Trusted Publishing (OIDC) over storing long-lived write tokens. If your account uses a security key/passkey and an older npm CLI only asks for an OTP, use a current CLI temporarily; it prints a browser confirmation link:

npx --yes npm@latest publish --access public --registry=https://registry.npmjs.org/

Verify after publishing:

npm view @your-org/plugin-my-plugin@1.2.3 \
  version dist.tarball dist.shasum dist.integrity \
  --json --registry=https://registry.npmjs.org/

npm view @your-org/plugin-my-plugin dist-tags \
  --json --registry=https://registry.npmjs.org/

Published npm versions can't be overwritten; every fix needs a new version number.

Register in the Plugin Market

The Market and npm are separate

The Botmux Plugin Market (https://github.com/botmux-ai/plugin-market) is a standalone static repository. It only stores discovery metadata, hosts no code, and is not a security endorsement.

Publishing to npm does not register the plugin in the Market;

Botmux currently does not read the Market index when installing: botmux plugin install <short-id> just expands to @botmux-ai/plugin-<short-id> by convention, so registered third-party plugins still need their full package name;

botmux plugin search, info, register, and publish are not implemented yet;

compatibility.botmux in a Market entry is metadata only; the installer doesn't check it.

Submit an entry

Make sure the npm package is publicly readable first. External contributors fork the Market repository:

gh repo fork botmux-ai/plugin-market --clone
cd plugin-market
git switch -c register-my-plugin

Add plugins/my-plugin.json:

{
  "id": "my-plugin",
  "package": "@your-org/plugin-my-plugin",
  "displayName": "My Plugin",
  "description": "One sentence on what problem the plugin solves.",
  "repo": "https://github.com/your-org/botmux-plugin-my-plugin",
  "docs": "https://github.com/your-org/botmux-plugin-my-plugin#readme",
  "categories": ["mcp", "productivity"],
  "compatibility": {
    "botmux": ">=3.8.0"
  }
}

Field	Rule
id, package, displayName, description, repo, categories, compatibility.botmux	Required
docs	Optional
repo, docs	Must be HTTPS URLs
categories	Each matches ^[a-z][a-z0-9-]{0,31}$, no duplicates
package	With the official scope it must be exactly @botmux-ai/plugin-<id>

>=3.8.0 is only a placeholder. Fill in the minimum version based on the Botmux capabilities your plugin uses and the versions you tested.

Build the index, validate, and open a PR:

npm install
npm run build
npm test

git add plugins/my-plugin.json index.json
git commit -m "feat: register my-plugin"
git push -u origin register-my-plugin
gh pr create \
  --repo botmux-ai/plugin-market \
  --head YOUR_GITHUB_USER:register-my-plugin

Replace YOUR_GITHUB_USER with your GitHub username. The PR must include both the entry file and the regenerated index.json; running only npm test without npm run build fails validation when the index is stale.

Security and release checklist

Installing a plugin means trusting its code:

npm installs may run package lifecycle scripts;

CLI, MCP, Dashboard, and Service code all run with the permissions of the system user running Botmux;

in production, install only packages from trusted publishers, pin exact versions, and verify registry integrity;

never pack tokens, cookies, private keys, browser profiles, logs, or user data into dist/;

don't let dist/ depend on repo source, the development directory, or undeclared global packages;

Market registration is a discovery channel, not a substitute for code review.

Before publishing, confirm:

npm ci && npm test passes;

dist/ is self-contained and runs without the source tree or node_modules;

npm pack --dry-run contains no sensitive files;

the manifest and every contribution entry pass validation;

the Service export's mode matches the manifest; a fixed port is set if you use slash commands or card callbacks;

both the local directory and the real tarball were installed and checked;

after publishing, version, dist-tag, and integrity were verified;

the Market entry passed npm run build && npm test, and the PR includes both the entry file and index.json.

References

Botmux source

Official plugin template

Botmux Plugin Market

Agent Chrome plugin example: a complete example that packs MCP, Skill, and Service into one plugin with per-session isolation

npm: Creating and publishing scoped public packages

npm: Trusted publishing

Keep sensitive results away from the model
The Market and npm are separate

Once installed, it can give the Agent Skills and MCP tools, add subcommands to the botmux CLI, add a page to the Dashboard, run a long-lived background service, and register Feishu /slash commands and card buttons. title: Prerequisites
content:
Before installing botmux, take a minute to check the items below. Most "installed but won't connect" or "sessions won't start" problems come from something missing here: the CLI isn't logged in, tmux isn't installed, or a command isn't on PATH.

Read this if: you'll run the botmux daemon (the background process) on your own machine (dev machine / devbox / server).

Skip this if: you only @ a bot in a group someone else already set up. You don't need to install anything locally.

Checklist

What you need	Required?	How to check
Linux or macOS (x64 / arm64)	Yes	uname -sm
At least one AI coding CLI, installed and logged in	Yes	Run it in a terminal (e.g. claude) and confirm you can chat
tmux	Yes, by default	tmux -V
A Feishu / Lark account	Yes	Used to scan the QR code that creates your bot
Node ≥ 22	Only for npm installs	node -v

Operating system

Linux and macOS are supported, on both x64 and arm64. On musl systems such as Alpine, the installer picks the musl build automatically.

On a Mac you can also use the macOS desktop app. It bundles its own runtime and starts with a double-click.

Windows: the daemon only runs on Unix-like systems. Install it inside WSL2.

botmux itself: no Node needed

The default curl install gives you a self-contained single-file program with its runtime bundled in. Installing and running it don't need Node.

You only need Node (≥ 22) in two cases:

You install with npm i -g botmux. That's npm's own requirement; once running, it behaves exactly like the curl install.

You develop plugins. Commands like botmux plugin init call npm.

AI coding CLI: at least one, working on its own first

botmux is just a bridge between Feishu and the CLI. It doesn't log in to the CLI for you. So:

Install the CLI you want, such as claude (Claude Code), codex, cursor-agent (Cursor), opencode, traex (TRAE CLI 2.0), agy (Antigravity), hermes, and so on. The full list is in CLI Adapters.

Make sure its command is on PATH (typing its name in a terminal finds it).

Run it once by hand in a terminal and confirm it can chat, then connect it to botmux.

Note: "botmux needs no Node" is about botmux itself. Many CLIs (like claude and codex) are npm packages and still need Node to install. Follow each CLI's own install guide.

tmux: the default session backend

A "session backend" is how botmux hosts the CLI process. The default is tmux. Its benefit is that CLI sessions stay alive and botmux can reattach to them after a daemon restart (see tmux Session Persistence).

Automatic install: when you run botmux start / botmux restart and tmux is missing, botmux first tries to install it for you (trying brew, conda, then the system package manager; it only asks for a sudo password when there's an interactive terminal). If that fails, it prints a manual install command.

If it can't be installed: when tmux is truly missing and your bots use the tmux backend, botmux start refuses to start and tells you to install it. When tmux is installed but doesn't work, the session is blocked and a card in Feishu tells you why. botmux never silently switches to another backend.

Version: the tmux 3.x shipped with common distros is fine.

Don't want tmux? Pick another backend explicitly: globally with the BACKEND_TYPE environment variable, or per bot with backendType in bots.json:

Backend	Notes
pty	No extra software, but sessions don't survive a daemon restart
herdr	Needs herdr; botmux can install it for you
zellij	You install zellij yourself
zmx	You install zmx (≥ 0.7.0) yourself, see ZMX Session Backend

Where to deploy

We recommend an always-on dev machine / devbox rather than a laptop. The daemon stays online, sessions stay alive, and you can control things from your phone anytime. After installing, run botmux autostart enable so botmux comes back up on its own after the machine reboots.

Common problems

Symptom	Cause and fix
botmux: command not found right after installing	The installer already added ~/.botmux/bin to your shell startup file, but you need to open a new terminal for it to take effect. Still missing? See Common Pitfalls
npm install fails and node -v is below 22	Upgrade to Node 22+ with nvm / fnm, or switch to the curl install and skip Node entirely
Sessions won't start, or the first message gets no reply	Usually the CLI isn't on PATH or isn't logged in. Get the CLI working by hand first, then see the FAQ
The CLI works in your terminal but botmux can't find it	botmux looks the command up through your login shell, but a CLI installed somewhere unusual can still be missed. Set cliPathOverride in bots.json to the CLI's absolute path, see CLI Adapters
botmux start says tmux is missing	Install tmux with the suggested command, or switch to another backend from the table above

Next: once everything is ready, go to the 5-Minute Quickstart.

title: Project Progress Card
content:
When you drive a multi-step project in an ordinary group, the coordinator bot can use botmux project to keep a pinned project progress card: goal, current focus, to-dos, blockers, milestones and the status of every subtask, all on one card that is updated in place instead of flooding the chat.

Project state is stored on the host, not in chat history. If someone withdraws the card, the next update posts a new one and pins it again.

Subtasks the coordinator sends out with botmux dispatch are registered on the card automatically, and progress that worker bots send back with botmux report is synced to the same card.

One group has one project and one card.

These commands are usually run by the AI itself. You tell the coordinator in the group "start project X" or "record that blocker", and it runs the matching command. The reference below helps you understand what it is doing; you can also ask it to run a specific command.

When to use it

What you need	Use
A project that runs for days, split across several bots, and everyone in the group should see progress at a glance	Project progress card (this page)
Just split a big task into parallel sub-topics; a Feishu task list is enough to track progress	Multi-topic collaboration
A bounded multi-step task that finishes with one deliverable	Workflow

They combine: once the group has a project, subtasks dispatched through multi-topic collaboration also show up in the card's subtask section.

Quick start

In an ordinary group, at the top level of the group (not inside a topic), @ the bot you want as coordinator:

@bot /project enable
That bot becomes the coordinator, and the other bots in the group managed by this botmux become workers (bots that can receive dispatched work). A "project group ready" guide card is pinned in the group. Only the bot's owner / allowedUsers can run this command.

Still at the top level, @ the coordinator and say what you want:

@bot Start the "Website revamp" project. Goal: ship the new home page within two weeks. Please break it down and drive it.
It's fine if the goal isn't clear yet. You can start with "I want to discuss…, help me clarify the problem and next steps first." Discussion is a valid project phase.

Once the coordinator creates the project, it posts a new project progress card at the current spot and pins it. The old guide card changes to "project started" and is unpinned. All later progress is updated on this card.

botmux project also works without project group mode, as long as you are in a session at the top level of an ordinary group (except in groups that ran /project disable or were set to "ordinary group" in the Dashboard). Enabling the mode adds two things: the coordinator receives a fixed "maintain project state" protocol every turn (read state → update whenever something changes → check the card before reporting), and dispatching is restricted to the worker list (see "Dispatch rules in project group mode" below). For the full /project usage see Slash Commands.

What's on the card

The card text is currently in Chinese; English names are given below.

Area	Content	Comes from
Header	Project title + status tag: in progress / completed	init --title, close, resume
Goal	The project goal	init --goal / update --goal
Current focus	What the coordinator is working on right now	--focus
Summary	e.g. "1 blocked · 2 in progress · 3 completed"	Computed from subtask status
In progress / Planned / Done	Subtasks grouped by state, each with an "open topic" link; Planned also lists items from --remaining	Subtasks + --remaining
Decisions / blockers	Numbered list of all blockers	--blocker, plus subtasks reported as blocked
Subtask status	Name, description, owner, status and topic link for each subtask	botmux dispatch / botmux report
Recent milestones	The latest 3 milestones and the "next checkpoint", collapsed by default	--milestone, --next-milestone

Subtasks have five states: pending, in progress, blocked, completed, failed. Blocked subtasks are listed first and completed ones last.

The table above describes the default "Status dashboard" template. With the "Compact list" template (see "Adjusting it in the Dashboard" below), the middle sections collapse into a one-line summary (summary · phase · next step), and subtasks become a one-per-line list.

Common tasks: want X → do this

What you want	Command
Create the project	botmux project init --title "Website revamp" --goal "Ship the new home page within two weeks"
See current state	botmux project status
Change phase / current focus	botmux project update --phase "Build" --focus "Wire up home page APIs"
Record overall completion	botmux project update --progress 40
Write down what's left	botmux project update --remaining "API integration; mobile layout; launch checklist"
Record a blocker	botmux project update --blocker "Waiting for design sign-off on hero colors"
Blockers resolved	botmux project update --clear-blockers
Record a milestone	botmux project update --milestone "Home page design finalized"
Set the next checkpoint	botmux project update --next-milestone "QA on Friday"
Finish the project	botmux project close --milestone "New home page is live"
Pick it up again after finishing	botmux project resume --phase "Phase 2" --focus "Add analytics events"

Full example: from kickoff to wrap-up

These are the commands the coordinator runs over the life of a project (you only talk to it in the group):

# 1. Kick off: only title and goal are required
botmux project init --title "Website revamp" --goal "Ship the new home page within two weeks" \
  --phase "Planning" --focus "Break down requirements and dispatch the first subtasks"

# 2. Dispatch: each subtask gets its own sub-topic and is registered on the card
#    (the title must be specific, at most 24 characters)
botmux dispatch ...   # e.g. "Home page frontend" to the frontend bot, "Home page regression" to the QA bot

# 3. While working: update promptly when the phase changes or a blocker appears
botmux project update --phase "Build" --focus "Wire up home page APIs" \
  --remaining "Mobile layout; launch checklist" --blocker "Waiting for design sign-off on hero colors"

# 4. Worker bots report from their own topics; the card syncs automatically
botmux report "Home page frontend done, preview link in the topic" --status completed

# 5. Blocker cleared, milestone reached
botmux project update --clear-blockers --milestone "Home page build done" --next-milestone "Launch on Friday"

# 6. Wrap up
botmux project close --milestone "New home page is live"

After close the card turns green and shows "completed": overall completion is set to 100, the phase becomes "completed", blockers are cleared and remaining work is set to "none". If you need to continue later, resume switches it back to "in progress".

Command reference

botmux project --help is the source of truth.

init: create the project

botmux project init --title <name> --goal <goal> [--phase <phase>] [--focus <current focus>]

--title and --goal are required.

--phase defaults to "planning" and --focus defaults to "break down and dispatch the first subtasks".

A group can only have one project. Running init again fails; use update or resume to keep going.

status: view state

botmux project status

Prints the full project state (JSON): goal, phase, blockers, milestones and every subtask.

update: make changes

botmux project update [options…]

At least one option is required:

Option	Effect
--goal <goal>	Change the goal
--phase <phase>	Change the phase, e.g. "planning", "build", "acceptance"
--focus <current focus>	Change "current focus"
--progress <0-100>	Record overall completion; must be an integer from 0 to 100. The number is only kept in the project state (visible in status); the card doesn't show it yet
--remaining <to-do>	Write down what's left; this replaces the previous value. Separate items with ； ; · or newlines; only the first 5 go into the card's Planned section
--blocker <blocker>	Add a blocker (duplicates are not added twice)
--clear-blockers	Clear all blockers
--milestone <milestone>	Add a completed milestone
--next-milestone <checkpoint>	Set the next checkpoint, shown in the milestone panel title
--clear-next-milestone	Clear the next checkpoint

--clear-blockers and --blocker can be combined: clear first, then add the new one.

close: wrap up

botmux project close [--milestone <completion note>]

Without --milestone, a "project completed" milestone is recorded.

resume: start driving again

botmux project resume [--phase <phase>] [--focus <current focus>]

Switches the status back to "in progress". Defaults: phase "continue", focus "resume project".

Common options

--json: print the full state instead of a short result.

--session-id <id>: target a specific coordinator session. Detected automatically when run inside a session, so you rarely need it.

How subtasks reach the card

Coordinator botmux dispatch ──► opens a sub-topic, assigns a worker ──► new subtask row on the card
                                                                          │
Worker runs botmux report --status ... in the sub-topic ─────────────────► row status / report updated

dispatch: every dispatched subtask adds a row with an "open topic" link and the assigned bots. It's "in progress" once the worker accepts, "pending" if it's only on standby (no task sent yet), and "blocked" if the dispatch wasn't accepted.

report: workers can add these options to update their row:
Option	Effect
--status	pending / in_progress / blocked / completed / failed. Defaults to in progress when omitted
--progress <0-100>	Completion of this subtask
--remaining <text>	What's left for this subtask
--milestone <text>	Add a milestone to the project

Reporting --status blocked puts the report text into the card's decisions / blockers list; reporting any other status later removes that blocker automatically.

To mark a subtask done, pass --status completed explicitly. The card does not guess completion from the report text.

For full dispatch / report usage see Multi-topic collaboration.

Dispatch rules in project group mode

After /project enable, dispatching is restricted so the card matches the real division of work:

Only the coordinator bot can dispatch, and only from its session at the top level of this group.

Work can only go to this group's workers, not to other groups.

Every new subtask needs a specific title of at most 24 characters; plain "subtask" (子任务 / 子项目) is rejected.

The worker list defaults to "automatically enroll new bots": bots managed by the same botmux that join the group later become workers. To keep the list strict, turn this off in the Dashboard.

Adjusting it in the Dashboard

Open Dashboard → Groups → a group's "Manage" → "Collaboration mode" (see Dashboard):

Switch between ordinary group and project group; pick the coordinator bot and dispatchable workers.

Progress card display: choose the "Status dashboard" template (with a subtask table, good for continuous monitoring) or "Compact list" (vertical summary, good on mobile); pick which modules to show (goal, blockers / decisions, subtasks and topic links, milestones); choose whether milestones are expanded by default. Saving refreshes the current card right away.

"Current project (read-only)" shows project status and how many subtasks are done.

This only controls how the card looks. Goals and progress are still maintained by the coordinator in the group. Each agent's responsibilities in the group can be set with @bot /project roles or Roles.

FAQ

"project 模式只能在普通群的 chat-scope 主控会话中使用" (project mode only works in an ordinary group's chat-scope coordinator session)
botmux project only works in a session at the top level of an ordinary group. DMs, topic groups and sub-topics inside an ordinary group are not supported. Go back to the group's top level and @ the coordinator.

project_mode_disabled
The group was explicitly set to "ordinary group": either in the Dashboard or by running /project disable. That turns project commands off. Switch it back to "project group" in the Dashboard, or send @bot /project enable.

project_coordinator_required
Another bot is this group's coordinator. @ the right coordinator, or have the current one run /project disable first.

project_already_exists
The group already has a project. Use update to keep going, or resume if it was closed.

Someone withdrew the progress card
No project data is lost. The next update (or subtask report) posts a new card and pins it.

If I leave project group mode, is the project kept?
Yes. /project disable only leaves the mode; project state and the progress card are kept. While disabled, botmux project commands are refused (project_mode_disabled) and the card stops updating; run /project enable again with the same coordinator to continue.

title: 5-minute quick setup
content:
Four steps and you're chatting with an AI coding CLI from Lark:

Step	Command / action	What it does
1. Install	curl -fsSL .../install.sh | sh	Installs a single-file program; no Node needed
2. Configure	botmux setup	One Lark QR scan: creates the app, sets permissions, and publishes a version for you
3. Start	botmux start + botmux autostart enable	Starts the background service and enables start on boot
4. Chat	Add the bot to a group and @ it	Pick a directory and the CLI gets to work

Before you start: take a quick look at the Prerequisites. The CLI you want to use (e.g. claude, codex) must already be installed, signed in, and working in a terminal; tmux is also needed by default. Most "installed but won't connect" problems come from something missing here.

Step 1 · Install

curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/deepcoldy/botmux/master/install.sh | sh

Open a new terminal afterwards and the botmux command is ready.

Supports Linux / macOS (x64, arm64). On musl systems such as Alpine, the musl build is picked automatically. On Windows, install inside WSL2.

Installs to ~/.botmux/bin/botmux; set BOTMUX_INSTALL_DIR to change it. The script verifies the download's SHA-256 and adds that directory to your shell's startup file (zsh / bash / fish).

botmux itself needs no Node. If your CLI is an npm package, installing that CLI still needs Node.

You can also install with npm: npm install -g botmux (this step needs Node ≥ 22). The npm package contains the same program and behaves exactly like the curl install.

On a Mac and want to start and stop the service with a click? You can also install the macOS Desktop App: it bundles its own runtime and shares the same ~/.botmux config with the command-line install.

Upgrading later:

Goal	Command
Upgrade to the latest (works for any install method)	Re-run the curl command above, then open a new terminal and run botmux restart
Already on v3.18.0 or later	You can also just run botmux update, then botmux restart
Install a specific version	curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/deepcoldy/botmux/master/install.sh | BOTMUX_VERSION=v3.18.8 sh

⚠️ BOTMUX_VERSION only takes effect when placed before the sh on the right side of the pipe. For releases older than v3.18.0, upgrade only with curl; see FAQ · How do I upgrade? for why.

Step 2 · Configure the bot

botmux setup

This is an interactive wizard: use the arrow keys to choose and Enter to confirm. Pressing Esc cancels setup without writing any config. On first run it asks you the following:

① Where the Lark app comes from

Option	Best for
One-scan create new app (recommended)	First-time users. Name the bot, then scan with the Lark app; botmux creates the app and retrieves the AppID/AppSecret
Select existing app	You've created apps before. After logging in, it lists your apps and fetches the credentials (Feishu tenants only)
Enter AppID/Secret manually	You already created an app in the Open Platform. You'll first choose Feishu or Lark (international)

After one scan on this machine, the login is remembered. Next time you add a bot, just confirm the account; no new scan needed.

② Pick a CLI: choose the CLI this bot connects to, e.g. Claude Code or Codex. You can type to search. If the CLI isn't found on this machine, you'll be told to install it first.

③ Where new topics start

Option	Effect	What to enter
Pinned default directory (recommended)	New topics start directly in this directory, no card	An existing directory, e.g. ~/projects/my-app
Repo selection card	Each new topic first shows a card to pick one of the scanned git repos	Scan root(s), e.g. ~/projects (searched 3 levels down; comma-separate several)

In repo-card mode, try not to use ~; there are too many folders to scan.

④ Admin (owner): when you create the app by scanning, the person who scanned becomes the admin automatically. When entering credentials manually, you fill it in yourself; a full work email is recommended, a phone number also works.

Once done, setup configures the Open Platform automatically: imports all permissions, sets the redirect URL, creates and publishes a version, then prints the result of each step.

🔧 When you need to finish Open Platform config yourself
You passed botmux setup --no-open-platform-auto (skip auto-config), or the auto-config failed.

setup then lists the remaining items (enable bot capability, long-connection event subscription, permissions, redirect URL, publish a version) with links; the full permission list is written to ~/.botmux/lark-scopes.json.

Choosing availability "Visible to me only" usually gets the version approved automatically.

Running botmux setup on a machine that's already configured shows a menu: Add new bot, Edit existing bot, Delete bot, Reconfigure. When done, run botmux restart as prompted.

Want to configure from a script or an AI agent instead of the interactive UI? Use the botmux setup add / botmux setup list subcommands; botmux setup help shows all options.

➕ Need permissions beyond the built-in list? Pass --extra-scopes-file <json> in scripted setup (Feishu tenants only; on Lark, add them manually in the developer console), e.g. botmux setup add --create-app --allowed-users <email> --extra-scopes-file ./scopes.json; for an existing bot run botmux setup configure <process-name|AppID> --extra-scopes-file ./scopes.json. The file uses the lark-scopes.json shape ({"scopes":{"tenant":[],"user":[]}}). {"scopes":[{"scope":"x:y"}]} is also accepted, but every entry in that form is requested as a user scope; use {"scopes":{"tenant":["x:y"]}} for tenant scopes. Scopes missing from the tenant catalog (including scopes that only exist for the other identity type) are skipped and listed in the result instead of failing the run. The file path is saved on the bot so later configure runs reuse it; if the saved file can't be read, setup warns and continues with the built-in list. Run botmux setup configure <process-name|AppID> --extra-scopes-file - to clear it.

👋 Welcome message on first launch: botmux setup add ... --welcome-message "Reply /init to get started" (or --welcome-message-file welcome.txt to read it from a file) makes the bot DM its owner once after it first comes online; for an existing bot use botmux setup edit <process-name|AppID> --welcome-message ..., and - clears it. Delivery is recorded under welcome-sent/ in the daemon data dir so restarts never resend; a failed send does not block startup and is retried on the next start. See bots.json · Welcome message.

Step 3 · Start

botmux start            # Start the background service (daemon)
botmux autostart enable # Start on boot (recommended; no sudo needed)

Start on boot uses user systemd on Linux and launchd on macOS.

The first botmux start asks which "feedback storage" to use. Just press Enter for the default SQLite. You can pick PostgreSQL here if you need it, and migrate later with botmux feedback storage (new tasks pause during migration; the original SQLite is kept, but botmux won't switch back automatically if PostgreSQL fails). See Feedback storage and migration.

Check status: botmux status; view logs: botmux logs.

Step 4 · Create a group and start chatting

Create a topic group in Lark (regular groups work too).

Group settings → Group bots → add the bot you just created.

@ the bot with a message, e.g. "@bot how do I build this project?".

If you chose the repo selection card in step 2, a card asks you to pick a project first; with a pinned directory, the CLI starts there right away.

The bot replies with a card that updates as it works and shows the full answer when finished:

Common questions:

Do I always need to @ it? In groups, the bot replies only when @-mentioned by default. In a group with just you and one bot, follow-ups inside a topic that's already started don't need the @. To go mention-free, see Mention policy.

Don't want a group? Just DM the bot.

Want to create a group in one click? Send /g <group name> in any chat, or open the "Groups" page in botmux dashboard and click "New Chat"; see Create a Session Group in One Step.

Not receiving messages? Self-check first

Most "no response" cases are local config or network issues. Let your AI CLI troubleshoot: it reads the logs, checks the config, and gives you a verdict.

First save the diagnostic task in a variable:

DIAG='botmux is not receiving messages in the Lark group. Diagnose read-only (do NOT change anything), run these in order and give the most likely cause + fix: botmux status (is the daemon running); botmux logs --lines 150 --no-follow (look for WebSocket connection failures, token/auth errors, permission errors 401/403/411/400, CLI spawn failures); cat ~/.botmux/bots.json (check AppID/Secret/CLI config); judge whether the long-lived WebSocket is blocked by a corporate network/proxy/firewall. Conclude at the end.'

Then run the line for the CLI you have (all non-interactive; they print the verdict and exit):

claude -p "$DIAG" --allowedTools "Bash"   # Claude Code
codex exec "$DIAG"                         # Codex
coco  -p "$DIAG" --yolo                    # TRAE CLI 1.0 / CoCo (legacy)
cursor-agent -p "$DIAG"                    # Cursor

The trailing --allowedTools / --yolo just let the agent run commands to read logs. botmux logs can pinpoint almost any problem.

Still stuck? Check by hand:

Symptom / suspicion	How to check and fix
Daemon not running, or config changed without a restart	botmux status to check, botmux restart to restart
Message didn't @ the bot	Groups require an @ by default; see Mention policy
Incomplete permissions, or a bot built from an old app (most common)	See Common Pitfalls; recreate via the latest botmux setup QR flow
Manually created app not fully configured	In the Open Platform: enable App features → Bot; receive events via long connection and subscribe to im.message.receive_v1, plus the card.action.trigger callback; publish a version
Long connection blocked (corporate network / proxy / firewall)	botmux logs will show connection errors

Run botmux restart after fixing. See FAQ / Troubleshooting for more.

Optional events: @ by editing, recall sync, disbanded groups

Missing any of these does not affect ordinary messages; only the related small feature. New bots subscribe to them automatically; for older bots, botmux tries to add them at startup using this machine's existing Open Platform login.

Event	Used for
im.message.updated_v1	Editing a message that didn't @ the bot to add the @, which then triggers a task
im.message.recalled_v1	In group context sharing (/context-sharing), marking recalled messages in the record. Only added when that feature is on
im.chat.disbanded_v1	Ending the bot's sessions in a group once it is disbanded (like /close: they can be resumed and worktrees are kept). Without it, those sessions are only closed at the next daemon restart

Things to note:

The startup top-up only adds events to the existing long-connection config. It does not change the delivery mode, change permissions, or publish a version. A log line saying the update request succeeded doesn't mean it's live. For production apps, review pending changes in the Open Platform, publish a version, then verify by editing a message that hasn't triggered the bot to add an @.

If the sender's chat access comes from team membership, an edited message also needs a contact lookup to get their union_id. This requires contact read permission (the default permission list includes contact:user.id:readonly) and the sender must be within the app's visibility scope. If the lookup fails, access is judged only by the original author's open_id; the editor's identity is never borrowed.

title: Session Relay
content:
/relay moves a running AI session to another group, another topic, or a DM, so you can keep going there.

What moves is the same CLI process and the same AI memory, not a fresh copy.

The Lark chat history stays where it was. The new place won't show the old messages, but the AI remembers what was discussed.

A typical case: work out a plan in your DM with the bot, then move it into the team group with one command so everyone continues from that context.

How it differs from Adopt: Adopt brings a CLI running in tmux on your computer into Lark. Relay moves a session that's already running inside botmux from place A to place B.

The two ways at a glance

I want to…	Send it in	Send
Pull a session from elsewhere into here	The target group / topic / DM	/relay
Move the current session into a new group	The current session	@BotA @BotB /relay --create [name]

/relay                                     # In the target place: pick a session from the menu and pull it in
@Claude @Codex /relay --create Plan review  # Create group "Plan review" and move the current session plus the collaborating bots
/relay --create                            # In a DM: create a group with just you and this bot

Option 1: /relay pulls a session in

Go to where you want the session to land (a regular group, a topic group, inside a topic, or your DM with the bot) and send /relay.

The bot replies with a picker card listing your own active sessions for the same bot, most recently active first.

Click a session to select it, then click "Confirm relay into this chat" ("Confirm relay into this DM" in a DM).

On success the card disappears and you see "✅ Relayed into this chat".

What the card shows:

Item	Meaning
Type / Where	Group chat, topic chat, or direct message, plus the group name
Status	🟢 Running / ⚪ Idle
Active	When the session last had a message
Search box	Search by title, group name, or path; search "dm" to find sessions in direct messages
Pages	5 per page; use "← Prev / Next →"

A few details:

Other topics in the same group are listed too, so you can move a session between topics of one group. Only the session already at the current spot is left out.

In a regular group (not topic mode) the card is visible only to you, so your session list isn't shown to the whole group. Inside a topic it appears as a normal reply in that topic.

Only the person who summoned the card can use it. Anyone else who clicks is told to run /relay themselves.

For a session that's busy, the confirm button reads "Session is running — cannot relay yet". Once it's idle, click the session again to refresh, then confirm.

Option 2: /relay --create moves into a new group

In the current session, send @BotA @BotB /relay --create [name]:

A new group is created with you and the @-mentioned bots.

The current session, plus the @-mentioned bots' sessions in this topic, move into the new group.

The original session gets a result message: the new group link and whether each bot moved successfully.

More notes:

The name is optional. Without one it defaults to "Session Relay MM/DD HH:mm". Names longer than 50 characters are cut off.

In a group you must @ at least one bot. The first @-mentioned bot creates the group; the others don't create duplicates.

In a DM no @ is needed (you can't @ other bots in a DM anyway). Just send /relay --create; the new group has you and this bot.

If a bot didn't make it (for example its session isn't yours, or its service is offline), the result marks it as skipped or not migrated. The new group is still created; send /relay there to pull that bot's session in.

What you'll see after a relay

The new place receives a notice:

📋 Relayed from "source group".
⚠️ Lark message history stays in the source chat; AI memory has been carried over.
@ the corresponding bot to continue.

In a DM, the last line reads "Just send a message to continue".

The original streaming card freezes as an archive with the status "🔄 Relayed away" and all buttons removed, so a stray click can't affect the session that's now live elsewhere.

Where the session lands

Where you send /relay	Where the session lands
Inside a topic	That topic
Top level of a topic group	A new topic started from the /relay message
Regular group (default flat mode)	The whole group
Regular group (set to open a new topic per @, or shared)	A new topic started from the /relay message
DM (default continuous mode chat)	The whole DM
DM (topic or group mode)	A new topic started from the /relay message

Switch group and DM modes with /reply-mode; see Slash Commands. For the different group types, see Session Model.

When relay won't work

Situation	What to do
You're not the session initiator (owner)	Only the initiator can move their own session; ask them to do it
The session is processing	Wait for the current turn to finish and go idle, then retry
No repo picked yet, so the CLI hasn't started	Go back to the original session and pick a repo first
The session was brought in via /adopt	Not supported. The CLI runs on your computer and botmux doesn't control its lifecycle
The target already has an active session for this bot	/close it in the target first, then relay
The session is closed	Closed sessions don't appear in the menu and can't be relayed

"Target already has a session" is judged by where the session would land: when landing in a whole group or whole DM, the whole group counts; when landing in a topic, only that topic counts, so different topics in one group don't collide.

If a relay times out or fails, the session is not lost. The chat history and AI memory are still in the original place; just click "Confirm relay" again a bit later.

title: Roles and Teams
content:
Give a bot a "persona" (Role): who it is in the group, what it's responsible for, and how it talks. The same bot can play different roles in different groups. The command is /role.

What's on this page:

I want to	Section
Give a bot a persona (global default / just for one group)	Set a persona
Control how often the persona is injected, reply privately to the asker, and other per-group switches	Per-group switches
Apply a set of personas to a new group in one go	Role profiles
Let other bots know "who's good at what"	Capability tags
One bot with several roles, each with its own memory (advanced)	Role switch

Set a persona

There are two levels:

Default role: the bot's persona in every group.

Group role: applies only to the current group and overrides the default role.

The order is always: group role > default role > none. For example, the same bot can be a "strict code reviewer" in group A, a "patient Q&A helper" in group B, and use its default role everywhere else.

With commands in the group

@-mention the bot in the group and send:

Command	Effect
/role	Show the persona in effect and where it comes from (group / default)
/role set <Markdown>	Set the group role; multi-line is fine
/role delete	Delete the group role and fall back to the default role
/role team	Show the default role
/role team set <Markdown>	Set the default role (the command keeps the old name team; it means "default role")
/role team delete	Delete the default role

Example:

/role set You are this group's technical advisor.
- Give the conclusion first, then the reasoning
- Flag risks before any production change

Personas are written in Markdown and injected into the CLI as a <role> block.

Each persona can be up to 32 KB (about 10,000 CJK characters); anything beyond that is truncated.

After a change, "every turn" mode picks it up from the next message; "only once" mode picks it up on a new or rebuilt session (see Per-group switches).

In the Dashboard

If you'd rather not type commands, open botmux dashboard:

What to change	Where
Default role	Bot Config page, each bot's "Default Role" section (same config as /role team set; saving it empty deletes it)
Group role	Role Management page → "By Group": expand a group, pick a bot, edit
Jump there from a group	Group Management page: in a bot's settings for that group, click "Edit chat role"

When you use "Duplicate" on the Group Management page to copy a group, you can tick "Also copy chat roles" to carry the source group's group roles (plus the per-group switches below) into the new group. Default roles are inherited automatically, so they don't need copying.

Per-group switches

On the Role Management page, select a bot in a group. Besides editing the persona, you can set the options below. Each is saved per "group + bot" and takes effect immediately.

Switch	Default	What it does
Injection	Every turn	"Every turn" sends the persona with every message; "Only once (first turn)" injects it only when a session starts or is rebuilt, which suits long personas and saves tokens. You can change the default per bot in the "Default Role" section of the Bot Config page, then override it for individual groups
Prefer private replies to the requester	Off	When on, the answer is sent to the asker in a private chat first; if that fails, it's posted publicly in the original topic. You can also set a "Group notice" (e.g. "Sent to you privately to avoid noise") shown in the original topic after a successful private reply; leave it empty for no notice
Topic task reporting mode	Off	See below

Topic task reporting mode: when this bot uses botmux dispatch in this group to hand a task to another bot, the assignee still uses botmux report to hand the result back to the dispatcher's session. With this switch on, the assignee also posts "completion + output location/summary" with botmux send --no-mention in the topic where it received the task, so people can see the result right in the group. It doesn't mention the dispatcher or open a new topic. --standby (reserve a bot without sending a task) doesn't involve this step.

In project groups, the coordinator bot also receives Botmux's fixed project-state protocol (for tracking progress and the pinned project card). It applies alongside the Role and is not affected by the Role's injection mode. For project groups, see /project in Slash Commands.

Role profiles

A profile is a reusable bundle of group roles: write a persona for each of several bots, save them under a name (e.g. collab-main), and apply them to a new group in one step later.

It's only a shortcut for writing: once applied, it becomes an ordinary group role. It doesn't add another persona layer and doesn't support template inheritance.

Commands

Command	Effect
/role profile list	List all profiles and show whether the current bot has its own entry
/role profile show <name>	Show the current bot's persona in that profile; add --all to see every bot's
/role profile set <name> <Markdown>	Write the current bot's entry directly
/role profile save <name>	Save the current bot's effective persona (group role, or the default role if there's none) into the profile
/role profile delete <name>	Delete the current bot's entry
/role profile apply <name>	Write the current bot's entry as the group role

Flags for apply:

--preview: preview only, write nothing.

--force: if the group already has a role, apply refuses by default; add this to overwrite.

--quiet: no reply on success (less noise when applying in bulk).

Notes:

Each bot only manages its own entry and never changes another bot's persona.

If the profile has no entry for the current bot, apply writes nothing and the bot keeps using its default role.

Profile names may only use letters, digits, ., _ and -, up to 64 characters.

In the Dashboard

Role Management page → "Profiles" tab:

Open or create a profile on the left.

In the middle, see which bots have entries; select a bot to edit its persona.

Under "Apply To Group", choose the target group and the bots to apply. Click Preview Apply first to check whether existing roles would be overwritten, then Apply Profile. Tick "Overwrite existing group roles" when you do want to overwrite.

Apply while creating a group

@botA @botB @botC /g --role-profile collab-main War Room

Once the new group exists, the bot that created it applies its own entry, then posts @botB @botC /role profile apply collab-main --quiet in the new group so the other bots apply their own entries.

Capability tags

A capability tag is a one-line self-introduction, such as "Good at frontend and UI review". It helps you and other bots pick the right one when collaborating.

/role cap set Good at frontend and UI review   # set
/role cap                                      # show
/role cap clear                                # clear

Tags are capped at 120 characters. One sentence is enough; use /role set for a full persona.

When other bots run botmux bots list to see who's in the group, they see each bot's tag.

Tip: put workspace: required / optional / none in the tag so dispatching bots know whether they must specify a repo or working directory when giving you a task.

Personas plus capability tags are the foundation of multi-bot collaboration: with clear identities and responsibilities, bots are less likely to get mixed up when @-mentioned in a group.

Teams: collaborating across machines

The Dashboard used to have a "Team" page; it has been removed. To work with bots on other people's machines, your machine needs to be connected to the central platform and be in the same team. Then use the command line:

botmux bots list --scope team: list bots that have joined your team.

botmux create-group --team <team> --agent <appId>: pull them and their owners into a new group.

Full steps are in the "Team scope" section of Multi-Bot Collaboration.

Role switch (advanced)

⚠️ Advanced feature: you need to deploy a "role library" first, and it currently supports Claude Code only. Deployment steps are in the repo's role-system deploy runbook. Below is how to use it once deployed.

/role above means "one persona per bot". Role switch gives one bot several full roles, each with its own persona and its own memory. Switch to "After-sales" and it carries the after-sales persona and experience that belongs only to after-sales; switch to "Product manager" and it's a different set.

Roles apply per topic; a new topic starts from the default role.

How to use it: just talk

You say	What the bot does
"switch role" / "what roles are there"	Lists the roles you can use (shared ones + ones you created), numbered for you to pick
"switch to After-sales" or reply with a number	Confirms and switches; from then on this topic is answered by that role, and the card footer shows the role name
"new role: Xiaohongshu ops, familiar with our brand voice"	Drafts a persona for you to confirm, then creates it and switches to it
"distill knowledge"	Turns the role's recent memory into structured knowledge stored back in the role (optionally as a Lark doc for human review)

Behind the scenes the model runs botmux role switch <role-dir>; you don't need to type it yourself.

Good to know

Separate memory: each role has one memory, shared across groups and topics, so it gets better at its domain the more it's used.

Context is kept: switching restarts the CLI and resumes the previous conversation; the new role's persona and memory load automatically when the new session starts.

Private roles are not a security boundary: "you only see shared roles and your own" is a convention in the role protocol file (_role-protocol.md) that the model follows. The daemon enforces only one thing: the target directory must be inside the role library ~/botmux-roles. It does not isolate roles per sender. If you need real isolation, add OS-level permissions yourself.

Not the same as /cd: /cd <path> (see Slash Commands) is the general "change working directory and restart", works with any directory, and needs operate permission. Role switch only moves within the role library.

The old command botmux cd has been renamed to botmux role switch. The old name now only prints an error and does not switch. When maintaining an older deployment, update _role-protocol.md in the role library to the new command.
